news.title: Trump’s Border Goons Spotted at Blue City’s Polling Site
news.text:
An elections supervisor in a heavily Democratic city says two Border Patrol trucks were parked at the city’s busiest early voting site on Monday.

Mark Earley, Supervisor of Elections in Florida’s Leon County, says he has filed a complaint with the FBI about the brief presence of federal agents at Northeast Branch Library in Tallahassee, the state capital.

“On Monday, October 19th at around 10:15 a.m., two Customs and Border Patrol vehicles parked at the Northeast Branch Library, our busiest early Voting site. This was shortly after the start of Early Voting here in Leon County,” Earley said. “The two vehicles appeared to stay for approximately 10 minutes before leaving the vicinity of the site.”

Earley said he has raised his concerns with local, state, and federal partners, whom he credited with being responsive. 

“I have lodged a formal complaint with the FBI, and to their credit, they are taking this seriously,” he added. 

Earley said intimidation and implied threats during the voting process are unacceptable.

“Voters should never experience intimidation from anyone when they are voting, and that includes being intimidated by law enforcement or any other governmental officials,” he said. “This nation belongs to the people. Government works for them. I will do everything in my power to ensure that our voters can vote in a fair election free from intimidation or implied threats.”

The Daily Beast has contacted the Department of Homeland Security, Border Patrol, ICE, and the FBI for comment.

Leon County is solidly Democratic. In the 2024 presidential election, Kamala Harris won by 11 points. As of Oct. 5, registered Democrats outnumbered registered Republicans by more than 30,000.

The sighting of federal agents at the Tallahassee voting site comes as DHS agents have been going door to door in several states, asking residents not only about their immigration status, but also whether they have registered to vote or voted in the past.

CBS News reported Wednesday that DHS agents are making these inquiries less than two weeks before Election Day. President Donald Trump claimed this summer that there were 250,000 people illegally registered—a number experts say is the result of false positives. Since Trump took office, CBS notes that only 156 people have been charged with voting fraud-related crimes.

Regional DHS accounts on X have been touting their efforts in places like northern California and in Kansas City.

In June, DHS launched a “surge” to seek out “criminal voter fraud” through Homeland Security Investigations, an arm of ICE, CNN reported. Internal department guidance said then that offices in nine states—Washington, Wisconsin, Missouri, Georgia, California, Pennsylvania, Nevada, New York and Connecticut—would launch investigations from early September to mid-October. “Overt” investigations so close to the midterms have typically been avoided because of a Justice Department policy against influencing elections.

But DHS is not required to follow the policy.

“While ICE Homeland Security Investigations is not able to comment on any active investigations, HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found,” a Homeland Security spokesperson told CNN then. “Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders.”

news.title: Republicans Dealt Triple Senate Polling Blow by Leading Election Forecaster
news.text: Democrats are ahead in three critical Senate races, according to new polling from The Cook Political Report on Wednesday, as Republicans fight to maintain control of both chambers this midterm cycle. The new report from Cook shows Democrat James Talarico up over Republican Ken Paxton in Texas by 5 percent, Democrat Josh Turek ahead of Republican Ashley Hinson by 2 percent in Iowa and Democrat Sherrod Brown leading Republican Jon Husted by 6 percent in Ohio. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. President Donald Trump won Iowa, Texas and Ohio during the 2024 presidential election versus then Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have recently slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. The polling lows come as Trump has crisscrossed the country in the lead-up to November 3 to rally for potentially vulnerable GOP candidates. Newsweek reached out to Paxton, Hinson and Husted's campaigns via email on Wednesday for comment. What Cook Political Report Shows The report from Cook highlights the narrow leads by the Democratic candidates amidst the fundraising advantage held by the GOP. The polling shows that all three Democrats are more trusted to handle corruption, inflation, as well as lowering gas and energy prices, Cook says. Republicans, on the other hand, have the lead on immigration and taxes. All three Democratic Senate candidates are "breaking even" in their favorability ratings compared to their Republican counterparts, who are all underwater by double digits, Cook notes. Similarly, Trump's net favorability is also negative, even in GOP stronghold Texas. “The economic center of the American electorate is collapsing on Republicans,” GOP pollster Greg Strimple of GS Strategies said in the report by Cook. “Voters are so upset with the lack of leadership on reducing their cost of living, they appear willing to propel Democrats to upset victories in reliably Republican states despite the fact that Democrats are less popular than either President Trump or Republicans. The level of voter discontent is truly unprecedented.” Cook concluded that overall Republican advantages have diminished as voters increasingly view the election adjacent to an unpopular president and connect their economic dissatisfaction to his policies. Robert Y. Shapiro, a professor of political science at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs, told Newsweek on Wednesday, "This is a good sign and confirms that Democrats are very competitive now for getting majority control of the Senate. If their turnout edge in early voting continues, even if somewhat less so, on election day, they would likely have a very good day and outcomes in the House, Senate, and certain races for governor." Grant Davis Reeher, a professor of political science at Syracuse University, also told Newsweek that the new polling is "the best snapshot that we have, but there are still a lot of known unknowns at this point." "How will the category of 'likely voters' differ from the actual voters? Will there be a 'coming home' phenomenon for Republicans frustrated with Trump and for Independents who voted for Trump in ’24? Are some people not admitting they will vote against the Democrat in Michigan, or that they will vote for the Republican in Texas, because they think it 'looks' bad?" Reeher added. "It’s not in the bank yet, except for Democrats taking the majority in the House. That is pretty much in the bank. But the Senate is still open," Reeher concluded. Cook's new polling, conducted by Democratic firm New River Strategies and Republican firm GS Strategy Group, interviewed 602 likely voters in Iowa, 959 in Ohio, and 934 in Texas from October 9-13, 2026. The margin of error for Iowa is 4 percent, 3.2 percent in Ohio and 3.2 percent in Texas. Iowa Turek leads in the poll over Hinson 46 percent to 44 percent as Libertarian Thomas Laehn landed 8 percent. Independents favor Turek 51 percent to Hinson's 27 percent, and 20 percent said Laehn. In the state's governor's race, Democrat Rob Sand leads 54 percent to Republican Zach Lahn's 43 percent and 3 percent don't know. Similarly, independents favor the Democrat 68 percent to Lahn's 26 percent and 6 percent don't know. Polling in the race has been a mixed bag, with both Hinson and Turek narrowly holding leads. In a co/efficient poll this month, Hinson had 48 percent compared to Turek's 45 percent. Two percent backed Laehn and 6 percent were undecided. The poll surveyed 863 likely general election voters from October 15-19, 2026, and had a margin of error of 3.32 percent. A YouGov poll showed Turek with 47 percent compared to Hinson's 46 percent, while 2 percent said someone else and 4 percent were undecided. The poll surveyed 2,245 Iowa likely voters from October 6-12, 2026, and had a margin of error of 3.1 percent. Cook rates the race as a toss-up as does Sabato's Crystal Ball. Prediction market site Kalshi shows Hinson in the lead on Wednesday afternoon with 57 percent compared to Turek's 43 percent. Polymarket shows Hinson in the lead 56 percent to 44 percent. Texas In the Lone Star State, Talarico leads Paxton 49 percent to 44 percent as Libertarian Ted Brown landed 3 percent and 4 percent don't know. Independents back Talarico 65 percent to Paxton's 23 percent, the poll shows. The governor's race is a different tune, as incumbent Greg Abbott leads Democrat Gina Hinojosa with 48 percent compared to 46 percent. Libertarian Pax Dixon has 3 percent and 3 percent don't know. The Senate race is rated as a toss-up by Cook and Sabato's Crystal Ball, as Talarico leads in a majority of new polling. An ActiVote poll shows Talarico with 51 percent compared to Paxton's 49 percent. The poll surveyed 400 likely midterm voters from October 17 to October 21, 2026, and had an average expected error of 4.9 percent. Similarly, a Marist University poll also showed Talarico up two percent with 47 percent compared to Paxton's 45 percent. Two percent said other, 4 percent were undecided and 2 percent did not respond. The poll surveyed 1,196 respondents from October 8-11, 2026, and had a margin of error of 4.9 percent for likely voters. Kalshi shows Talarico in the lead on Wednesday afternoon with 67 percent versus Paxton's 33 percent. Polymarket shows Talarico with 67 percent compared to Paxton's 34 percent. Ohio Brown leads Husted 49 percent to 43 percent, Cook's polling shows. Three percent also backed Libertarian William Redpath, and 4 percent backed Independent Greg Levy. Independents preferred Brown with 60 percent versus Husted's 24 percent. Similarly, in the gubernatorial race, Democrat Amy Acton leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy 49 percent to 44 percent, while 6 percent backed Libertarian Don Kissick. Recent polling shows a close race with Brown leading in a majority of polls. Cook rates the race as a toss-up along with Sabato's Crystal Ball. An ActiVote poll shows Husted with 50.2 percent compared to Brown's 49.8 percent. The poll surveyed 400 likely midterm voters from September 26 to October 18, 2026, and had an average expected error of 4.9 percent. A Marist University poll shows Brown with 48 percent compared to Husted's 44 percent, while 2 percent said other, 4 percent were undecided and 1 percent did not respond. The poll surveyed 1,176 respondents from October 15-18, 2026, and had a margin of error of 4.5 percent for likely voters. Kalshi shows Brown with 67 percent compared to Husted's 33 percent. Polymarket shows Brown with the majority at 70 percent compared to Husted's 31 percent. Beyond the life-or-death stakes for Ukrainians, the spat has forced many Republican officials to spend precious time criticizing the administration instead of Democrats. But the bigger story is that Trump’s long-standing affinity for Russia may finally be coming back to bite him in a meaningful way.

Back up: Last time you wrote about this, Trump was buying Russian diesel and criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. What’s happened since?

A lot. Last week, Trump signed an executive order immunizing Russia from new sanctions under a law Congress passed to punish Putin’s aggression. On Monday, the Washington Post revealed that the administration is holding up interceptor missiles Ukraine needs to defend against Russian attacks. On Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk may have conspired with Trump to throttle Ukraine’s access to SpaceX-made battlefield satellites. (“Some fools still think the legacy news is real. Amazing,” Musk wrote today on X in what read like a classic nondenial denial.) And on Wednesday, Steve Witkoff, the president’s real-estate buddy turned globetrotting negotiator, visited Russia and praised Putin, an autocrat who invaded a neighboring country and has reportedly ordered the assassinations of domestic political opponents, for his humanity. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Witkoff said. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that.”

How are Republicans reacting? 

Not well! “WTF, Steve?” Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina posted on Wednesday. “Another embarrassment,” wrote Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska. While campaigning in Maine, Sen. Susan Collins said Trump should reverse his decision to waive sanctions on Russia.

It’s true that those lawmakers are frequent Trump critics, but the backlash is starting to break containment. Rep. Max Miller of Ohio, a former Trump aide who has likened himself to the president as he fights domestic abuse allegations, labeled Witkoff’s bootlicking “ridiculous.” Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania called for an investigation into whether Musk slowed Ukraine’s satellite access, calling it “likely a violation of the law.” Putin “is not our friend, and he is certainly no humanitarian,” wrote Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa. “His relentless attacks on innocent civilians in Ukraine show his total disregard for human life.” As the Wall Street Journal’s conservative editorial board thundered on Sunday, “When the election is over there needs to be a bipartisan reckoning for Mr. Trump’s budding alliance with the Kremlin against Ukraine, Europe and American interests.”

Speaking of the election: Neither Trump nor his party would seem to benefit from a public spat. So why are they doing this?

To some extent, Trump may think he’s helping. He blames Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for the high cost of diesel. It’s actually Trump’s war in Iran that caused the spike, but importing Russian fuel could help save vulnerable GOP candidates if it eases prices even a little. Witkoff’s praise also came after Putin agreed to release a 74-year-old American whom Russia had detained for years. Meanwhile, Collins, Fitzpatrick, and other Republicans in tough races may earnestly care about Ukraine. But they also stand to benefit politically from shivving a president whose approval ratings keep setting new lows.

OK, but if they really wanted to stop him, couldn’t Trump’s Republican critics in Congress … you know, do something?

Yes. Worse, Congress has enabled some of Trump’s steps to betray Ukraine. The sanctions law he sidestepped—named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, a longtime Russia foe—contained language that let Trump exempt Russia. As a result, some Democrats had refused to support the bill. A bipartisan majority of Congress, most of them Republicans, passed it anyway.

Trump has gotten away with cozying up to Putin for a decade now. So should we really expect his party to pay a price now?

It’s fair to wonder. During the 2016 campaign, Hillary Clinton memorably argued that Trump would become Putin’s “puppet.” Enough voters overlooked those warnings to give Trump the White House and Republicans unified control of Congress. In 2024, Kamala Harris predicted that Trump would “give up” Ukraine. Again, Trump and his party won anyway.

But this time really could be different. Polls suggest Republicans are struggling to motivate their voters, and an election-eve GOP-on-GOP fight probably doesn’t help. The president has also taken the less popular side. Americans as a whole support Ukraine less uniformly than they did when the war began, but more Republicans than not still like Zelensky more than Putin, favor aiding Ukraine, and back sanctions against Russia. Faced with backlash, Trump could try to change course; as we’ve explained, he has repeatedly flip-flopped on Ukraine. But with millions of Americans already casting early ballots, any turnabout might come too late to make a political difference.

Before we transition to some happier reads, an update on yesterday’s newsletter: After Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign twice declined to tell us whether it was behind an ad featuring his gubernatorial opponent’s estranged mother, the Ohio Republican has admitted that his campaign made the ad—and plans to spend $4 million airing it statewide. So as ugly as that race looked yesterday, it could get uglier still.

OK, time to pivot. If you’re in search for some evening enjoyment, my colleagues think you should:

Mark your calendar for a special Slate event: This spooky season, the midterm elections are full of frights, but Slate’s politics team is here to warn you about any jumpscares. Join senior political reporter Jim Newell, politics (and Slatest!) editor Patrick Reis, and Mary Harris and Lizzie O’Leary of What Next and What Next: TBD for a live Zoom event on Thursday, Oct. 29, to discuss what’s real, what’s noise, and what to expect next. See you there!

Tune into a sharp new TV show: The creators of The Good Wife and The Good Fight have spent years skewering Big Tech. Their new series, Cupertino, is laser-focused on how Silicon Valley is undermining America’s laws and values. Slate’s Sam Adams talked with creative duo Robert and Michelle King about how they made exactly the right show for our current moment.

Peer into one of social media’s dark corners: Family estrangement is one of the most complicated situations to navigate for parents and children alike. When writer Christina Wyman discovered that her mother was active in a Facebook group for estranged parents, she found herself in a toxic echo chamber that was doing more harm than good. Listen to her story on the latest episode of ICYMI.

Give your brain a workout: Who is a “philosopher associated with deontology and zero-effort puns” (four letters)? Who “played Ahnold’s twin in Twins” (five letters)? Solve these clues in today’s crossword.

Congrats! You’re more than halfway through the week. Enjoy the night and see you tomorrow.

As Russia launched its biggest attack since the invasion, Musk “capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network, the people said, rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless,” the Journal said.

It’s unlikely Musk acted alone. Reuters reported last week the decision to sabotage Ukraine came from the White House, the implication being it was Donald Trump’s. But Musk said publicly that the administration did it. Administration sources said publicly Musk did it. Common sense says both did. The Journal said Musk’s team contacted the White House to “coordinate messaging.” A source told the Telegraph: “The reality is that they were both in it.”

Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, is acting like what’s been done can’t be undone. He has put up with Trump’s humiliation tactics for years to maintain access to weapons and intelligence he needs to liberate his country. But now, he is no longer biting his tongue.

“People have to hear reality,” Zelensky said. Whether it’s lifting old sanctions on Russia, waiving new ones or sandbagging Starshield, it illustrates Trump’s affinity for dictators, he said, and that Trump has taken the wrong side of history in deciding to help Vladimir Putin.

US Senator Chris Murphy, of Connecticut, told Anderson Cooper that Ukraine was winning the war over the course of the last year, despite Trump’s refusal to maintain previous levels of support, until Putin “called in a favor, using whatever lever he has over the president.”

Murphy called recent choices by the White House, including last night’s decision to withhold Patriot missile shipments to Ukraine, “a pattern of behavior” in which the president "has decided he’s gonna put Ukraine in a position where they may be pressured to capitulate … a strategy to put Russia in the most powerful position possible to gain a settlement.”

While Trump deserves to be treated as if he has crossed a line, so does Musk. The fact of his involvement in a conspiracy to destroy Ukraine’s sovereignty should trigger a credibility crisis. Indeed, Heather Cox Richardson compared him to none other than Benedict Arnold.

“Musk’s decision to change the course of a war with ‘a seeming flick of a switch,’ taking it upon himself, with or without the complicity of White House officials, to reverse the foreign policy of the United States of America for the benefit of Russia’s president Vladimir Putin, is a stunning assumption of power reminiscent of Revolutionary War general Benedict Arnold’s weakening of the Americans’ defenses and draining of supplies at the strategic fort at West Point to enable the British to capture it before he was discovered and defected,” she wrote.

Musk seems aware of the possible consequences of showing his whole ass. "After what was described as a ‘night of carnage’ in Kyiv because of the blackout," the Telegraph reported, Musk "had been alarmed about the possibility of adverse consumer reaction in Europe.”

I would guess his fear is rooted in more than concern for his companies, government contracts and profit margins. He has made an enemy out of a sovereign nation whose fate is bound to those of others allied in the most powerful security apparatus on the planet. Governments protect men like Elon Musk. They are how he became an alleged trillionaire. But government protection becomes optional in times of war. Zelensky needs Starshield. He doesn’t need Musk. If I were an oligarch like him, I would be careful around open windows.

In America, among the Democrats, there’s growing apprehension about Musk’s "stunning assumption of power." “If it’s one man, Elon Musk, who is dictating our foreign policy, then he puts the United States at enormous risk,” US Senator Elizabeth Warren, of Massachusetts, said today. “He’s the one who decides whether Ukraine, out there fighting on the frontlines to protect its democracy, lives or dies? No. We should not have one man in that position.” 

The Times reported last week that if the Democrats regain control, they might investigate Musk’s AI interests, his foreign entrenchments and what he did as head of the Department of Government Efficiency. His role in a conspiracy against Ukraine adds another item to the list.

Politico reported this week that the House Democrats are already coming up with a game plan for when they have the subpoena power. Texas Congressman Greg Casar said “our committees need to be doing oversight both into the Trump administration, but I think even more importantly or equally importantly, into the corporations and ultrarich people who have tried to corrupt our government. And, of course, Elon Musk is on that list.”

In the spring, the Democrats introduced a bill that would unwind mergers made in the second Trump administration. More generally, the Democrats are focused on anti-monopoly enforcement and price-fixing amid a cost-of-living crisis, as well as political graft. Musk’s former position at DOGE yielded hundreds of billions in contracts. He got out of federal investigations and avoided billions in fines. His companies constitute a virtual trust.

And the Democrats are in the mood for trust-busting.

Filmmaker Alex Gibney made a documentary about Musk that shatters his reputation as a genius inventor. He told Piers Morgan last night that contrary to popular belief, Musk has never invented anything. His real genius is stock pumping, Gibney said. “That is where he really shines. He’s managed to take companies, which have a rather mediocre profit-and-loss record, and make himself through stock pumping the richest man in the world.”

Stock pumping is market manipulation. It’s illegal under federal law and New York state law. I’m reminded of that time when Tucker Carlson asked Musk what would happen to him if Kamala Harris won the 2024 election. “How long will my prison sentence be?” he said.

It’s hard to avoid the conclusion that Musk understands the stakes – that he has crossed the line, that there’s no going back, and that all that’s left is to pour hundreds of millions into the midterms in the hopes of staying out of jail. He is the single biggest backer of Ken Paxton, the corrupt and impeached attorney general of Texas. He is literally trying to buy a senator.

No one elected Elon Musk. A majority of the governed did not grant him authority over them. He has no constituency beyond Twitter followers. He has demonstrated unconscionable disloyalty. If he can pull the plug on Ukraine’s defense, he can pull the plug on America’s.

news.title: Xavier Becerra tried to jail me for the crime of reporting
news.text:
California gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra says his campaign is a “break the glass” moment for the state.

I should know. 

During his time as California Attorney General, Becerra tried to put me in jail for exercising my basic First Amendment rights.

Specifically, he charged me with the “crime” of undercover video reporting on the harvesting and sale of aborted baby body parts.

In other words: He tried to make journalism illegal.

Becerra’s predecessor in that office, Kamala Harris, launched the unprecedented case under California’s law restricting video recording of “confidential” conversations. It was the first and only time that law has been used against newsgathering.

On her watch, in 2016, the state launched an armed raid on my home to seize my undercover footage.

But it was Becerra who, in one of his first acts in office, made the decision to file 15 felony charges against me under the video recording law. 

Almost a decade before the California establishment launched the “Stop Nick Shirley Act” to stop citizen journalists from investigating fraud, Becerra was a key architect in early efforts to shield politically-favored, government-funded wrongdoers from scrutiny.

Even left-leaning outlets called Becerra’s filing of charges “a disturbing overreach” to protect a politically-favored interest group, namely Planned Parenthood.

As the case dragged on, half the charges against me were thrown out. Two Southern California companies exposed by my undercover reporting admitted illegally selling body parts in a nearly $8 million settlement with local law enforcement.

But Becerra persisted, even arguing that exceptions in California’s video recording law for gathering evidence of crimes did not apply because legal abortion, in his view, meant that partial-birth abortions and even infanticide of an infant born alive during an abortion were not crimes against a “person.” 

It was not until the Congressional release of some of the Harris-seized tapes, and the reelection of President Donald Trump, that Becerra’s successor, Rob Bonta, finally negotiated the dismissal of the case.

Becerra carried his selective regard for the law into his tenure as U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) during the Biden administration. Under oath before Congress, he repeatedly denied the very existence of the federal Partial-Birth Abortion Ban Act — while eliminating important ethics safeguards for fetal experimentation.

Candidate Becerra now also boasts about his role injecting “700 million COVID shots into the arms of Americans”. We now know that Becerra’s HHS enabled Dr. Fauci’s cover-up of the potential miscarriage risk to pregnant women from COVID shots in the first trimester.

Two years ago, my investigative reporting nonprofit exposed gruesome public records documents from the University of California’s fetal organ harvesting program with Planned Parenthood in San Diego, dating from the time that Becerra was prosecuting me for reporting.

Among the documents were the “consent forms” that Planned Parenthood had used to sign late-term abortion patients up for the UC organ harvesting program — both the English-language version, and the Spanish-language translation. 

The English-language forms disclosed to pregnant women that there might be “commercial value” in Planned Parenthood and the University’s harvesting of their baby body parts. But the Spanish-language forms removed the disclosure about “commercial value” entirely.

Xavier Becerra doesn’t want journalists to report on what he actually does. When he sat down with a journalist in May, he tried to tell her what she was allowed to ask him. “This is a profile piece, this is not a gotcha piece,” he instructed.

Take it from me: Becerra won’t stop there in his attempt to control the narrative. People talk about threats to the media. He’s the real deal. 

He’s right about one thing: This really is a “break the glass” moment. The First Amendment is at stake in this election.

David Daleiden is the founder and president of The Center for Medical Progress.

news.title: Abandoning Jewish Voters Could Cost Democrats Dearly in November
news.text:
I recently wrote about how the Democrat Party is bleeding Jewish support as its far-left wing seizes control and drags the party toward antisemitism and open sympathy for Palestinians, Hamas, and Hezbollah. It will likely cost Democrats dearly in November. Kamala Harris won about 71% of the Jewish vote in 2024, making Jewish voters one of the most dependable parts of the Democrat base, but a growing share of them are clearly troubled by the party’s direction, and some are doing something they've never done before.

Take Michigan's Senate race. According to New York Times reporter Jeremy Peters, a Michigan native who grew up near Democrat nominee Abdul El-Sayed's hometown, lifelong Jewish Democrats in the Detroit suburbs are voting Republican for the first time. Peters argued the shift hurts El-Sayed and points to a midterm that falls short of the blue wave Democrats rode in 2018.

"That's a big deal," Peters told MS NOW's Morning Joe. "I don't know of any other marquee race in the country right now where the Republican candidate is converting Democrats."

Peters found it remarkable that Democrats are worried enough about El-Sayed to back former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), especially in an environment he described as tough for the president.

"I mean, given the overall environment for Trump, the economy, prices, the war, gas, all that, like, it's very unusual and really quite striking that there are Democrats who are so concerned about their party's nominee that they're willing to vote for the candidate who's aligned with Donald Trump," he said.

Better yet for Republicans, the polls may be missing it.

Peters noted concerns that Michigan surveys are oversampling college-educated voters, who form El-Sayed's base, and that first-time GOP crossovers are keeping quiet.

"But people also, from what I'm hearing, are somewhat reluctant to tell a pollster that they're going to be voting for a Republican for the first time in their lives," he added.

Recommended: A Pollster Just Admitted Faking Its Numbers, and The Fallout Is Huge!

This was a predictable problem. Back in August, former Clinton pollster Mark Penn flagged the danger after El-Sayed barely survived his primary against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), even though polls had projected a landslide. Penn calculated that if just 5% of Stevens' voters defected, Rogers would likely win.

"It is highly likely that you're going to find 5% of those Steven voters who are going to switch to the other side. And that alone would give a margin of victory to Rogers," Penn told Fox News.

This isn't limited to El-Sayed's race either.

Last week on CNN News Central, CNN's Harry Enten walked host John Berman through the collapse in New York, where Jewish voters make up a larger share of the electorate than in any other state.

In Siena polling, Andrew Cuomo carried Jewish voters by fifty-five points in the 2018 governor's race, and Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-N.Y.) won them by fifty-one in 2022. This year, her lead has shriveled to thirteen points. That's a 38-point swing toward the GOP in a single term.

The generic House ballot tells the same story. Democrats led among New York Jewish voters by forty points in 2018 and forty-nine in 2022. This year's polling average has them up by only thirteen.

"Their lead has absolutely tumbled into the Hudson River among Jewish voters. Yes, they are still ahead, but we are talking about historically strong numbers for Republicans among Jewish voters," Enten explained.

That shift could rescue Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), whose 17th District has a large Jewish population and went for Kamala by less than a point. Prediction markets give Lawler a 39% chance of holding the seat, which makes him an underdog, but a live one in a year when Democrats expect to dominate New York.

Enten said Lawler's competitiveness alone "is an indication that Jewish voters, if in fact they vote the way that the polls say, they may just save Mike Lawler's seat in Congress for him."

Democrats have a knack for taking their loyal constituencies for granted, and it’s coming back to bite them once again.

news.title: TV Star Offers Weird Excuse After MAGA Posts
news.text:
Orange Is the New Black star Natasha Lyonne is trying to convince her fans that she’s “not MAGA” after posting that she “prefers Trump.”

Lyonne, 47, confused fans with a couple of posts, including sharing a string of emojis that appeared to support Trump’s praise of Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Tuesday. Hours after rampant fan speculation, the star reposted a fan who called her pro-Trump posts “sarcasm.” 

She argued that she assumed the posts on her account, which has over half a million followers, would go unnoticed.

“#MakeAmericaGayAgain 🏳️‍🌈🏳️‍⚧️🐝😎 sorry—thought these were just murmurs into the ether—didn’t realize it was a whole thing,” she wrote.

In another post, she replied to a fan who wrote, “So is Natasha Lyonne MAGA now or am I misreading her posts?” 

“Not MAGA,” she wrote succinctly. 

She told one fan that speculation about her political leanings was “Legit all bulls--t,” and shut down another who wrote, “Ohhhhh motherf---er… not you too,” in response to her pro-Trump posts. “Fine, I’ll delete them, but this was funny,” she wrote. 

The now-deleted posts include the emoji message, “🚀🫡☀️😎” in a response to Trump’s praise of Elon Musk. “A BIG THANK YOU to our legendary friend, @ElonMusk, for his incredible generosity in giving SpaceX Stock to millions of American children through TRUMP ACCOUNTS!” Trump wrote, which Lyonne appeared to salute with her message.

The other removed post included a clip of Vance using a vile smear to dismiss a protester at a rally. Lyonne wrote at the time, “Sketchy mofo—prefer Trump—this s--t is even scarier.” Initially, the American Pie star said little to clarify when a fan asked what she meant by “Prefer Trump,” writing, “To insert Manchurian Candidate here?”

Lyonne, also known for roles in the Netflix series Russian Doll from 2019 to 2022 and Peacock’s Poker Face from 2023 to 2025, has been open about her struggles with sobriety. In January, she shared on social media that she had relapsed after nearly a decade. 

In April, she was escorted off a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York amid claims that she appeared disoriented and flouted flight attendants’ takeoff instructions. She later apologized, saying she had taken a sleeping pill.

Posts from her peeved fans over her pro-Trump posts mirrored those of previously “apolitical” comedian Nate Bargatze, who posed with MAGA royalty at Trump’s UFC birthday party in June. Bargatze then refused to comment on the vile slurs made against Michelle Obama at the event. “Damn, it sucks to see someone you like publicly reveal themselves to be a complete self-oblivious idiot…Welp, you’ve lost a fan,” one fan wrote to Lyonne. 

The responses also echo those aimed at Rozonda “Chilli” Thomas, one-third of 1990s R&B girl group TLC, who reposted a conspiratorial post about Michelle Obama and was later discovered to have made donations to MAGA causes. (Thomas later denied being MAGA, saying the donations were to “support the veterans,” and that the reposts were an accident.)

Lyonne, a registered Democrat, fundraised for the party on social media in 2020 and endorsed Kamala Harris in 2024. She told The Hollywood Reporter last February that she was “pretty horrified” by Trump’s rise.

news.title: Trump vs the press: The president has a long history of attacks on the media from personal abuse to billion dollar lawsuits
news.text:
Donald Trump’s relationship with the media has long been combative with the president routinely dismissing reporting he does not care for as “fake news,” launching personal attacks on reporters and issuing outright bans for journalists in his orbit.

His latest clash involved an outburst at The Independent’s Andrew Feinberg in the Oval Office Tuesday after taking exception to a line of questioning about whistleblowers exposing government fraud. Feinberg was part of the reporting pool in the room and drew Trump’s ire on multiple occasions. That led Trump to lash out. 

“I don’t know who the hell you are, but you better be careful,” the president said, before subsequently calling him a “sick person” and adding: “I actually think there’s something wrong with you.”

The episode was one of Trump’s many battles with the press - here is a look back at his ongoing feud with the people who cover him : 

Trump attacks directed at The Independent drew rebuke online with commenters noting the president’s attitude.

“Trump seems to be getting increasingly unhinged. He's a megalomaniac whose power is slipping away, which is a dangerous combination. If the Republicans lose the midterms and he is even more contrained [sic], we could be in for a perilous couple of years as he abuses his executive powers to lash out,” one social media user noted.

Another user questioned what Trump meant in some of his attacks. 

“The question is.. What does he mean when he makes the statement ‘You better be careful?’” one Instagram user stated. 

While some people were quick to back the president and called it a ‘privilege’ to be in the White House, others defended journalists for doing their jobs by asking questions to the president. 

“Well done for standing up to the Bullies,” one wrote. “It is good to see reporters challenging Trump on his lies. It would be funny if every reporter asked the same question if one of them is silenced. I find Vance more irritating because he behaves like a school boy bully who likes to join in when the bully leader has nothing to say except try to silence those who challenge him.”

The president has had multiple clashes with the women of the press corps, notably snapping “Quiet, piggy!” at Bloomberg’s Catherine Lucey last year and telling Weijia Jiang of CBS News she would be “incapable” of “acing” a cognitive test as he claimed he had just done. 

He has also called Karen Travers of ABC News “very loud,” her colleague Mary Bruce “a terrible person and a terrible reporter,” Katie Rogers of The New York Times “ugly, both inside and out” and asked Nancy Cordes of CBS News: “Are you a stupid person?”

One of his most frequent targets has been Kaitlin Collins of CNN, who he has repeatedly urged to smile more and even called “stupid and nasty.” 

Most recently, Trump quite literally swatted away another female reporter’s question about his comments on the prospect of Iran bombing Los Angeles and San Diego and almost blew up at another until he found out she was from the right-leaning Daily Wire, after which he was much more courteous. 

In a memorable encounter aboard Air Force One in May this year, Trump called New York Times correspondent David Sanger “treasonous” for asking about what the benefit would be of repeatedly bombing Iran.

“I had a total military victory,” Trump answered testily. “But the fake news, guys like you write incorrectly. You’re a fake guy… I actually think it’s sort of treasonous what you write, but you and The New York Times and CNN I would say are the worst.”

During his first term, CNN’s then-White House correspondent Jim Acosta had his press credentials revoked after being falsely accused of pushing an intern at a briefing, leading to a disagreement over a doctored video and a short-lived lawsuit before his access was restored. 

The White House tends to adopt the same tone as the president both in its briefings and public statements, characterizing the media as unrelentingly hostile to the administration and disingenuously negative in its outlook.

“President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses from the fake news media,” spokeswoman Lauren Bis recently told The Independent when asked about the prospect of House Democrats launching new investigations into Trump after the midterms, to give just one example. 

Often calling out the Fourth Estate broadly, their attacks can also take a more direct turn, as when White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung reacted to questions about Katie Zacharia’s farewell social media posts by saying: “The Independent breathlessly obsessing over an innocuous photo is a prime example of how much thought rot they are experiencing due to a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome that has warped any sense of reality in their pea-sized brains.”

Pundits have long warned that Trump’s attacks on the press serve to undermine trust both in the outlets themselves and in the media more generally, potentially weakening its capacity to hold the powerful to account, a very necessary democratic function.

Jonathan Chait of The Atlantic argued recently that the president’s attempts to shoot down all awkward questions also serve to block him off from useful criticism that might give him pause for thought and lead him to make better decisions, rather than simply yielding to his impulses.

The president has also attempted to revoke access to networks and outlets he considers unfriendly to his administration, moving in September to “ban” journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds. 

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States,” he huffed on Truth Social when announcing the measure.

The major networks responded by banding together to suspend their shared TV coverage of Trump’s events until the trio were reinstated, an important show of unity. 

U.S. District Judge Tim Kelly then ruled that the president must welcome back the three outlets, finding that the ban had likely been unconstitutional. The White House duly did so. That did not stop Politico from being barred from the presidential plane earlier this month. 

All of which followed the Associated Press, one of America’s oldest and most respected news wires, being thrown out after refusing to change its style guide to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as “the Gulf of America” in accordance with Trump’s preferences, a restriction it successfully overcame in court. 

The president has launched a series of legal challenges against coverage that angered him, notably suing CBS over its editing of a 60 Minutes interview with his 2024 election rival Kamala Harris, The Wall Street Journal over a report about a birthday doodle he allegedly sent to Jeffrey Epstein and the BBC over a package on the Capitol riot from an episode of Panorama.

Paramount, CBS’s parent company, was criticized after choosing to settle Trump’s complaint for $16 million in July 2025, despite the network’s lawyers describing his arguments as “meritless” in court filings. 

In April this year, Florida District Judge Darrin P. Gayles dismissed the president’s $10 billion defamation suit against the Journal over the letter, the existence of which was first reported by the newspaper prior to its being recovered from the Epstein estate by Democrats on the House Oversight Committee as part of their investigation into the late pedophile. 

Gayles found that Trump had failed to demonstrate that the article in question was published with “actual malice,” saying he came “nowhere close to this standard.” The president has denied writing the letter and has not formally been accused of any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

The $10 billion BBC case is ongoing, with lawyers for the British media corporation most recently asking a federal judge to force Trump to sit for a deposition.
news.summary: The president has complained about ‘fake news’ ever since he first ran for high office in 2015. Joe Sommerlad reports on Trump’s second term attacks on the Fourth Estate

news.title: Neil Bush, Bush Family Back Far-Left James Talarico in Texas Senate Race
news.text:
Neil Bush, the brother of former President George W. Bush, posted on Facebook that he voted for far-left Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race.

Bush, who holds a number of business interests in China, said of Talarico, “I have been enormously impressed by the way he approaches complicated and controversial issues.” Neil is the latest member of the Bush family to publicly support Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton.

“My vote was motivated by two things: deep concern about Ken Paxton’s record and genuine admiration for the character and principles I see in James Talarico,” Bush said in the post, claiming President Donald Trump and those who have “enabled him” have “done enormous damage to the Republican Party.” He also said he disagreed with Paxton’s concerns over the conduct of the 2020 election.

Bush also said of Talarico, “His faith appears to be a deeply rooted source of humility, compassion, and conviction.” In earlier reporting by Breitbart News, Talarico’s church in Austin is led by Rev. Jim Rigby, who said he welcomes atheists to join his church and, “If you hate religion, we’re on the same team.” 

Talarico called Rigby “my pastor in every sense of the word,” adding he was one of “the biggest influences on me as a Christian, as a human being.” In another report, Rigby questioned whether Jesus actually rose from the dead in an Easter sermon.

Neil Bush is most famous for being sued by the FDIC and federal regulators for “gross negligence” following the collapse of Silverado, a Denver-based savings and loan association, in which he ultimately paid a hefty fine.

The admission that the long-time Republican voted for Talarico is the second recent announcement from the Bush family in support of the Democrat.

Barbara Bush, the daughter of the 43rd President, donated to a super PAC supporting Talarico; in 2024 she had campaigned in support of failed presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

As for the former President, George W. Bush headlined a fundraiser in support of several Republicans running for the U.S. Senate including Sens. Susan Collins, Jon Husted, Dan Sullivan, and challengers in open seats — Ashley Hinson, Mike Rogers, John Sununu, and Michele Tafoya. Paxton was notably not one of the beneficiaries of Bush’s support.

news.title: Democrats furious after pollster boosting far-left candidates admits fabricating surveys: ‘Absolute scumbags’
news.text: Democrats are up in arms after a so-called polling firm that projected far-left candidates as strong contenders in several primaries admitted that it had fabricated its polling data. Wedgewood Polling, which billed itself as an election survey company, released a statement Tuesday night admitting it used "fabricated numbers" for an "experimental project to demonstrate the vulnerabilities, lack of oversight, and overall low barrier to entry in the modern political polling industry." The group's polls were cited by Abdul El-Sayed's campaign amid a high-profile primary race against Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. The nonpartisan polling aggregator Political Polls also cited Wedgewood in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, showing socialist Francesca Hong having an edge over Republican candidate Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis. McMorrow said Wedgewood's numbers led to her donations drying up and reporters having "hounded" her with calls to drop out of the race. JONATHAN TURLEY: FAKE POLLSTER'S STUNT WAS A RECKLESS GAME WITH REAL RACES "Sure, a point was proven. Polling is broken. But tens of thousands of people poured their hearts, time, energy, hard-earned money into something they believed in - for a year-and-a-half, and it was treated like a game," she said in a statement on X. "Trust is already at an all-time low. We don't get out of this mess without rebuilding trust. And media - who loves to ride the drama of a pollercoaster - needs to take a hard look at what's legitimate and what's not." Unlike El-Sayed, who advanced from Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Hong lost Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary to the establishment-backed candidate. El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is currently locked in a tight race against former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., for Michigan's open Senate seat. Democrat strategist Jennifer Holdsworth said she ran a super PAC that raised money for McMorrow and that "this poll was used by several donors to pull back funding at a time we were being outspent by $80 million." MORNING GLORY: THE POLLS GOT MICHIGAN BADLY WRONG. NOW DEMOCRATS MAY FACE A BIGGER RECKONING Wedgewood's numbers were cited by high-profile outlets like The New York Times and Decision Desk HQ, which both said they have since removed them from their projections. The Times said it removed 15 polls released by Wedgewood between June and October after it admitted to fabricating data. The outlet said Wedgewood had "answered a series of questions regarding the identities of the pollsters; the methods they were using to draw their sample, contact respondents and weight their polls; and the source of their funding" during its vetting process. Decision Desk HQ said it removed 17 Wedgewood polls from its projections but that it "has not changed the projected seat totals or chamber control probabilities in the Senate or House." Wedgewood Polling's statement said it "was never intended to sway an election" but rather was aimed as a "wake-up call" about data integrity and vetting standards. MYSTERIOUS POLLING FIRM BEHIND FAKE ELECTION SURVEYS CLOSES AFTER ADMITTING ‘SOCIAL EXPERIMENT’ "These people are absolute scumbags," veteran Democratic strategist and former Kamala Harris advisor Mike Nellis told Fox News Digital. "They can try to claim that they have some moral high ground here, but they lied about their polling data, got caught, and are freaking out because they've committed fraud." "The people responsible for this should be run out of American politics, and if they can be, they should be prosecuted to the full extent of the law," Nellis said. He added that both Democrats and Republicans, as well as the media, should reflect on how polling is verified "because there's likely other people that are doing things like this." TOP ELECTION SCHEMES ROILING KEY MIDTERM RACES AS BOTH PARTIES ACCUSE RIVALS OF TRICKERY Independent outlet FiftyPlusOne said it was investigating Wedgewood when it had released its statement. Co-founder G. Elliott Morris wrote on X, "We were investigating Wedgewood for faking their data and emailed them for comment this morning, ahead of publishing the findings tomorrow. They are trying to cover up their fraud with the 'we were doing a social experiment' excuse." Former Obama staffer Tommy Vietor said on X that Wedgewood's actions amounted to "lying and fraud." A group called "Wedgewood Polls" had also previously created a GoFundMe to raise money for polling in Nebraska's gubernatorial and Senate races. It raised $500 of its intended $5,000. "I know they crowdfunded, I believe, a good chunk of their polls," Nellis told Fox News Digital. "Are they going to return that money? And if not, are they going to be prosecuted?" FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON Other Wedgewood surveys showed Democrats with significant edges over Republicans in states like Texas, where a July Wedgewood poll showed James Talarico leading state Attorney General Ken Paxton among Hispanics by 64% to 30%. Republicans, including President Donald Trump, have long heaped doubt on the veracity of polls. Polls notably showed former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton with an edge over Trump in 2016 — far from the actual result. And with the fight for control of Congress coming to a head in November, every data point is being scrutinized as political tea leaves. news.title: Polls Show Democrats Making Gains in Key Senate Races
news.text:
With the midterm elections about two weeks away, Senate Republicans are finding themselves playing defense in some unexpected places as Democrats continue to chip away at their hold in the polls.

Most observers have expected that Democrats would reclaim the House—boosted by historical trends such as the presidential “six-year itch” that favor the out-of-power party and by diminishing approval for congressional Republicans since 2025.

But few observers expected Democrats to reclaim the Senate following Republicans’ sweep of the upper chamber in 2024, when the GOP picked up four seats for a total of 53 in the upper chamber.

That’s changing as Democrats make polling gains in key Senate races.

Here’s what to know.

Perhaps the most watched race of the entire cycle is in Texas, where Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has maintained a consistent and compelling lead over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton across the election cycle.

Related StoriesMahmoud Khalil Asks Supreme Court to Hear Challenge to Detention RulingSupreme Court to Decide Fate of Reconstruction-Era Home Distilling Ban

Democrats in the Lone Star State have dreamed of “turning Texas blue” for decades.

They had a close call in 2018, when Democratic nominee Beto O’Rourke came within around 2.5 percentage points of unseating incumbent Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas).

Then, in 2024, President Donald Trump swept the state by 14 points. For many Democrats, that seemed to be the end of their hopes to flip the state.

But now, the Senate race in Texas is devouring Republican funding as Talarico has consistently led in polls, with downstream effects on funding for Republicans across the country.

Both parties have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the race, between the contentious Republican primary earlier this year and the general election fight.

Talarico has built a campaign based on his values as a liberal Presbyterian seminarian and on his track record as a state legislator, leading in 18 out of the 19 polls conducted since July. Paxton has led in a single poll conducted by Emerson College.

In a sign of the party’s growing electoral woes, Republicans in early October pulled funding out of former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley’s Senate race against former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper entirely.

Polls have shown Cooper favored this cycle, leading in every poll since July 2025. Cooper leads by around 9.2 percent, based on an average of the six most recent polls.

In Georgia, Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is favored by polling to hold onto his seat in the blue-shifting state, leading Republican nominee Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) by 7.6 percentage points in an average of five recent polls.

As the Atlanta metropolitan area has grown, the state as a whole has trended increasingly toward Democrats in recent years, beginning with President Joe Biden’s shock victory over Trump in 2020. In 2024, Trump reclaimed Georgia by Republicans’ lowest margin of victory in the Peach State since 1996.

While the Senate race remains competitive, it’s clear to many that the state is slipping out of Republicans’ reach this year.

Meanwhile, the party is moving funding to western states that had previously been presumed safe.

There are also warning signs for Republicans in Great Plains states such as Kansas and Nebraska.

Kansans have long been known in national politics for their deeply Republican voting tendencies.

But in recent years, some observers began to notice a rising purple streak in the state’s national voting habits that could boost Rev. Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist megachurch pastor and author who’s making a competitive showing in polls against incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas).

Marshall is an obstetrician-gynecologist who was first elected in 2020 after beating out a crowded primary field. He’s been the subject of controversy in the state after The New York Times reported that he had sued hundreds of his former patients, leading to 81 arrests due to missed court dates.

Marshall has decried the report as a political hit job, saying he used standard billing practices and maintaining that he has delivered thousands of babies free of charge to lower-income families.

The race was originally rated lean Republican by Cook Political Report, which now rates it a toss-up. Although Marshall led in the first poll taken of the race released on Sept. 11, every poll since has shown him either tied with or running behind Hamilton, and Republicans are worried.

The funding pulled from North Carolina has been pushed into the Kansas race by national Republicans. Trump spoke in support of Marshall at a rally just north of Wichita on Oct. 19.

In 2020, key population centers such as Shawnee County—which houses Topeka, the capital—and Riley County backed the Democrat in the Senate and presidential races for the first time since the 1970s.

Much will come down to Johnson County, a Kansas City suburb lying just west of the border with Missouri, and by far the most important single county in the state’s electoral politics, making up around one-fifth of the state’s entire population.

For years, it’s been shifting left, backing both Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris in the previous two elections.

In Nebraska, independent candidate Dan Osborn—who made national news during his close campaign against Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) in 2024—is making another bid for the office.

This year, he’s running against incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), and polls have shown a tight race. In surveys taken in September and October, Ricketts led by 4 and 5 points, respectively. Osborn led by about the same margin in polls taken in May and September.

Republicans maintain a structural advantage in the state. Although 53 percent of registered Nebraska voters live in rural areas, the urban and suburban population in Nebraska is reliably Republican—but has potential to swing in line with an anti-Republican national environment.

Omaha is a crucial decision-maker in the race, as its population has trended away from Republicans in recent cycles, voting for Harris in 2024.

In another surprising shift, Republicans are moving $5 million into Sen. Darline Graham’s (R-S.C.) race against physician Annie Andrews.

Graham was appointed to the seat by outgoing Gov. Henry McMaster earlier this year, following her brother’s death in July.

The $5 million investment into the race is significant as the state has rarely needed such funding from the national party in the past, though it’s not an amount that signals alarm.

Currently, Graham leads in all three polls taken of the race, but the margins are surprisingly narrow in a state that backed Trump by around 18 percentage points just two years ago.

On average, Graham sits at 44.7 percent in polls. Andrews, running as a moderate Democrat in the Republican stronghold, has 43.3 percent support, trailing Graham but well within the margin of error.

Trump is scheduled to visit the state as part of his blitz of midterm campaign rallies.

A federal judge has been suspended because fellow judges concluded she has mental health problems that interfere with her work. U.S. District Judge Ada Brown “suffers from a temporary or permanent mental condition that interferes with her ability to perform the responsibilities of her office,” a Fifth Circuit panel found.

Columbia University graduate and pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil wants the Supreme Court to prevent the Trump administration from re-arresting and deporting him under an existing removal order. Matthew Vadum has more in his latest report.

Actress Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS). Despite learning that she does not have the condition, Applegate said her physical difficulties remain unresolved, leaving her uncertain about what has been causing her health issues.

France has been rocked by violent, destructive protests in recent days, and more may be coming. Etienne Fauchaire is on the ground with his latest report.

Trump said this week that he was open to holding a trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss denuclearization. “If Xi wants to have it, I’d have it. I’m sure we'd talk about other things like trade too,” Trump said.

—Stacy Robinson

news.title: Nepo MAGA Senator’s Nightmare Deepens With Grim Downgrade
news.text:
Republicans have hit the panic button as a Trump-backed senator’s chances of holding onto her late brother’s seat have been downgraded for the second time in weeks.

The Cook Political Report, which tracks campaigns and elections across the country, has shifted its analysis of the South Carolina Senate race from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican.”

And GOP insiders have started pointing fingers as Sen. Darline Graham’s gaffe-filled campaign begins to derail even further.

“There’s no question that there’s a drag at the top of the ticket,” one told MS NOW on Wednesday. 

It comes as Trump is scheduled to host a rally in Clemson on Wednesday evening in a bid to shore up support. “I will be heading to South Carolina for a BIG Rally this evening,” he wrote in a Truth Social post earlier in the morning. “Darline Graham is GREAT!”

Republicans rallied around Graham, 62, after she stepped in to fill the seat vacated by Sen. Lindsey Graham’s death earlier this year. 

But officials are now downbeat about her prospects after a series of blunders on the campaign trail, including admitting she knows virtually nothing about the foreign policy issues her brother made the centerpiece of his 34 years in office.

“There are voters who are voting third party, there are the voters who are voting elsewhere, and there doesn’t seem to be as much cohesion amongst the Republican electorate around her,” the insider told MS NOW.

Tuesday’s downgrade of Graham’s lead is the second time in as many months the Cook Report has shifted the seat away from the GOP in a state Trump, 80, carried by almost 18 percentage points over Kamala Harris in 2024.

Latest numbers suggest Graham is currently ahead of her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews by a polling average of only 2.7 percentage points just 12 days out from the Nov. 3 vote.

Graham has delivered some dismal debate performances, such as trying to blame Democrats for starting Trump’s war with Iran and failing to explain the U.S. strategic significance of Taiwan.

“I’m not that informed on national security,” she said during her primary run in August. “National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise.”

It’s a stark departure from her late brother’s role as one of the foremost foreign policy hawks in D.C. 

Lindsey Graham repeatedly lobbied for foreign military intervention, including demands for strikes against Iran years before Trump launched the current conflict, as well as a 2022 visit to Taiwan to champion support for the island against Chinese aggression.

“It’s political malpractice that we’re even having to spend money in the state,” the GOP official said to MS NOW on Wednesday about the current senator’s chances of holding on to the seat.

“South Carolina should not be a state where we have to spend money to shore up a Republican nominee,” the official added. “That money is better used in other states, but we are here, and this is the cards that we have to play right now.”

Those concerns reflect a wider pattern driven by Trump’s plummeting approval ratings, which hit 31 percent on Monday, marking the lowest of either of his terms. 

The downward spiral has turned once-safe Republican seats into increasingly competitive races as Democrats charge toward the November race for control of the House and Senate with an almost 9-point lead in those polls.

Trump has insisted that his supporters should imagine he is personally running for re-election, hoping it will drive higher turnout among the remaining MAGA faithful. 

The Daily Beast has contacted Graham’s campaign for comment on this story.

news.title: As midterms loom, Democrats learn to speak a new language: American
news.text:
“I’m a border security Democrat.”

With five words at a CNN and Jubilee Town Hall last week, Texas Senate candidate James Talarico sought to dodge the stigma of the Biden administration’s failure to secure the southern border.

Talarico is one of a crop of Democratic midterm election candidates choosing language that pivots away from past election failures. For future political viability, the Democratic Party must reclaim voters alienated by its perceived contempt for politically and culturally more conservative Americans — including those who were once the foundation of its blue-collar base but defected to President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.

One way to do this is to craft messaging on issues like affordability that connect with working Americans and highlight the link between Trump’s decisions — like the Iran war — and the cost of groceries, gasoline and housing.

Democrats also face a linguistic minefield as they try to again talk like the voters they want to attract without angering the party’s new base of more liberal urban and highly educated voters.

In recent years, Democratic messaging has often seemed academic, esoteric, politically correct or choked with jargon. Terms like “unhoused people” and “birthing people” were adopted to include and respect people who are marginalized or vulnerable. Such language shows regard for the humanity and individual rights of others. But it has sometimes obscured meaning and baffled people who are not deeply political, or turned away voters with more conservative values.

In some cases, Republicans have used Democratic language to drive a wedge between the party and persuadable voters and to suggest it has tacked to the left. The most hard-hitting ad of the 2024 election season attacked Democratic nominee Kamala Harris over transgender issues, telling voters that “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.”

The term “defund the police” became a national slogan after the murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. Republicans soon co-opted it to argue that Democrats were weak on law and order — a narrative that circulated for several elections, even though senior party members like former President Joe Biden publicly repudiated it and its policy implications.

And in one of the most notorious examples of loose language haunting Democrats, 2016 nominee Hillary Clinton suggested some Trump fans belonged in a “basket of deplorables” — handing MAGA a rallying cry to underscore Trump’s claim that establishment elites viewed his voters with disgust.

‘I understand why you voted for Trump’

One reason — apart from Trump’s unpopularity — why Democrats are competitive in more states than expected during this year’s midterms is that they’ve selected candidates who sound like their states.

In North Carolina, Senate nominee Roy Cooper has developed a colloquial way to argue he’d “Make Stuff Cost Less.” He appears to be rebuilding the broadened coalition that made him governor twice in a reliably Republican state.

Talarico speaks the language of faith in pious Texas to distinguish himself from progressive Democrats. His “border security Democrat” phrase balances his support for both a hard border and a softer immigration purge that would target only undocumented criminals rather than “small business owners, grandmothers and infants.”

In Iowa, which Trump won by double digits only two years ago, Democratic Senate nominee Josh Turek brands himself a “prairie populist” and tells voters, “I understand why you voted for Trump” before he lambasts the president for raising costs and starting the kind of war he vowed never to fight.

In Maine, Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson refused to apologize for telling Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during a debate. The incumbent Republican suggested he was guilty of sexism. But Jackson, a former logger, turned the conceit of supposed establishment contempt for working people against his opponent. He said on CNN’s “State of the Union” Sunday that, “What I’m not going to be is talked down to by Senator Collins.”

Jackson added: “I’m fighting for Mainers. And, I mean, I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me.”

Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has meanwhile developed his own searing linguistic critique of Trump that links alleged White House corruption to the economic struggles of millions of Americans. “Under the failed president Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, stock your fridge, visit the doctor or power your home,” Ossoff said at a rally earlier this month. “They promised to drain the swamp. Instead, it’s the most corrupt administration of all time, and everybody knows it.”

Of course, Democrats have one big advantage that facilitates their linguistic balancing act: It’s far easier to find language to attack an incumbent Republican president over high prices and economic insecurity than it was for the party to defend the Biden administration for its struggles on the same issues in 2024.

And a party that failed to take advantage of a president who boasts about an economic “golden age” when Americans are paying $4.30 for gasoline and dread their grocery bills would be guilty of gross political incompetence.

‘Talk like a normal human’

In August 2025, the moderate think tank Third Way published a memo warning that the while Democrats spent “billions of dollars trying to find the perfect language to connect to voters” they used “an awful lot of words and phrases no ordinary person would ever dream of saying.” The memo concluded that “the effect of this language is to sound like the extreme, divisive, elitist, and obfuscatory, enforcers of wokeness. To please the few, we have alienated the many—especially on culture issues, where our language sounds superior, haughty and arrogant.”

In the wreckage of another defeat to Trump, some top Democrats agreed.

Former Obama administration White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, a possible 2028 presidential candidate, told CNN’s Michael Smerconish a year ago that in 2024, the party allowed itself to be framed as “culturally, not only distant, but culturally isolated from where the general public is.”

Emanuel added: “You have to build a winning coalition, which means it has to be big. It has to be broad, and other voters have to be respected, something elements of our party don’t do. They like to lecture people to be exactly like them.”

Another possible Democratic presidential candidate, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, has been striking similar notes this year. He said at a dinner in Michigan that he was a “pro-diversity” governor but that to win, Democrats needed to “talk like a normal human.”

He criticized terms like “food insecure” for hungry and “justice-involved population” instead of prison inmates. “Sometimes these terms make it feel like we’re talking down to people, like we’re talking at them, instead of to them,” Beshear said.

Matt Bennett, executive vice president of public affairs at Third Way, said Democrats this year were doing a better job of finding ways to connect with voters.

“For the most part, we’re delighted with the people that have won their primaries and the races that they’re running, and they seem very well suited,” he said, pointing especially to the example of Cooper, who has prospered in a state that last voted Democrat for president in 2008. “He has done what it takes to win the trust of these voters.”

The general election campaign has been kinder to Democrats so far than primary season, which threw up several viral moments quickly seized upon by Republicans to portray Democrats as extremists.

In an interview with Fox News, Democratic Socialists of America co-chair Megan Romer advocated abolishing the Senate, replacing the presidency and the Supreme Court, and defunding the Pentagon. She said prisons could be abolished under long-term plans, along with national borders. The encounter ran on a loop on conservative media for days as the GOP tried to define all Democrats by association.

But Republicans are now creating their own viral moments with language that seems deliberately aimed at excluding citizens and groups.

Trump has been inciting Islamophobia in the crudest and most inflammatory terms by mocking the name of Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayedand falsely calling him a jihadist. On Monday, Vice President JD Vance suggested that a protester — a person of color who shouted that he was an American citizen — must have crossed the border illegally.

Democrats may not be the only party with a language problem.

news.title: Comment on Biden Believes Putin Has Made Decision to Invade Ukraine by เทปใส OPP
news.text:
U.S. PRESIDENT Joe Biden says Russian President Vladimir Putin has made up his mind to invade Ukraine.

“I’m convinced he’s made the decision. We have reason to believe that,” Biden said during remarks from the White House on Friday afternoon.

Earlier in the day, the Russian military announced that Saturday it will hold massive drills of its strategic nuclear forces, which Putin will personally oversee. However, Biden said he doesn’t believe Putin is seriously contemplating the use of nuclear weapons.

Biden called out the shelling of a kindergarten by Russian-backed fighters in the Donbas region, which Moscow said was carried out by Ukraine. He pointed out other disinformation he said Moscow was peddling to the public, including claims of a genocide in Donbas and a Ukrainian attack on Russia.

“All these are consistent with the playbook the Russians have used before to set up a false justification to act against Ukraine,” Biden said. For weeks his administration has warned of such pretext scenarios and “false flag operations.”

Should Moscow invade Ukraine, it will be critical for the United States to convince the world that Russia is the aggressor and that it did so unprovoked, Max Bergmann, senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, told VOA.

Ukraine: What We Know

“This was a master class from the Biden administration in how to win an information war with Russia,” Bergmann said. “The Biden administration has read the Kremlin playbook and they are exposing Russian disinformation as they come across it.”

However, Biden is still offering Putin a de-escalation off-ramp, saying that diplomacy is “always a possibility.” He said, based on the “significant intelligence capability” of the U.S., he has reason to believe Putin will still consider the diplomatic option.

U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken is scheduled to meet in person with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Feb. 24.

Meanwhile Washington and its allies are analyzing a document that the Kremlin delivered to U.S. Ambassador John Sullivan in Moscow. It is Russia’s written response to the recent U.S. and NATO offer to negotiate over their missile deployment and troop exercises in Europe while rejecting Russia’s demands related to possible Ukrainian membership in NATO.

Russian cyberattacks

During a White House briefing Friday, Anne Neuberger, deputy national security adviser for cyber and emerging technology, said for the first time that the U.S. believes Moscow was responsible for recent so-called DDoS cyberattacks on Ukraine.

“We believe that the Russian government is responsible for widescale cyberattacks on Ukrainian banks this week,” Neuberger said. “We have technical information that links the Russian Main Intelligence Directorate, or GRU, as known GRU infrastructure was seen transmitting high volumes of communication to Ukraine-based IP addresses and domains.

“This recent spate of cyberattacks in Ukraine are consistent with what a Russian effort would look like and laying the groundwork for more disruptive cyberattacks accompanying a potential further invasion of Ukraine sovereign territory,” she added.

While noting there are no specific threats on the U.S. homeland at this point, Neuberger warned that administration officials are bracing for any Russian cyberattacks on American targets following the imposition of sanctions on Moscow.

The U.S. is “taking the necessary actions to prepare and harden potential U.S. targets against what might come next,” said Nina Jankowicz, a global fellow who studies disinformation and cybersecurity at the Wilson Center. She spoke to VOA.

Talks with European allies

Biden delivered his remarks after his latest round of urgent talks with European leaders and a call with a bipartisan group of members of Congress who are representing the United States, along with Vice President Kamala Harris, at the Munich Security Conference on the Ukraine crisis.

“Despite Russia’s efforts to divide us at home and abroad, I can affirm that has not happened,” Biden said. “The overwhelming message on both calls was one of determination and resolve.”

However, there are differences among allies on the timing and severity of sanctions against Moscow. For example, the initial package will likely not include banning Russia from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) system used by 200 countries to handle international financial transfers.

“We have other severe measures we can take that our allies and partners are ready to take in lockstep with us, and that don’t have the same spillover effects,” said Daleep Singh, the deputy national security adviser for international economics, who spoke to reporters during the same White House briefing Friday. “But we always will monitor these options and we’ll revise our judgments as time goes on.”

Singh said U.S. measures are not designed to reduce Russia’s ability to supply energy to the world but that it would be “a strategic mistake” for Putin to retaliate against Western sanctions by cutting back energy supplies to Europe.

“Two-thirds of Russia’s exports and half of its budget revenues come from oil and gas, and if Putin were to weaponize his energy supply, it will only accelerate the diversification of the world away from Russian energy consumption,” he said.

Singh added Moscow would be unable to replace technology imports from other countries, including China, if Washington also imposes tough export controls that it has threatened.
