news.title: Obama, Harris lean into 'Gazamaxxing' as Black voters focus on America for the midterms — not the Mideast
news.text: African Americans may be more supportive of U.S. backing for Israel than we are hearing about, at least according to a recent Fox News Poll — but you wouldn’t know it from the attention-seeking antics of some of their most prominent political and cultural "leaders." Last week Barack Obama was in Northern Ireland, where — in between saluting his own regional peace-making accomplishments — the former president accused Israel of "taking" Palestine from Palestinians during the Jewish nation’s founding back in 1948, according to a report in the Jerusalem Post. Just a few days earlier, failed presidential candidate former Vice President Kamala Harris spoke at a conference in Korea, where she blasted both the current administration and her onetime boss, President Biden, for their "failure to use our leverage to curtail the Israeli government’s horrific conduct in the war in Gaza." WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM And let’s not forget grievance and grift-master Ta-Nehisi Coates, who appeared on a recent Vanity Fair podcast where the writer partially blamed Harris’ 2024 defeat on her unwillingness to speak out more forcefully against America’s engagement in Gaza — or being someone, as he described, who "did not have the courage of [her] convictions." All three missives come, uncoincidentally, at the tail end of a midterm election cycle in which Black voters have unexpectedly emerged as potential king-makers in the Democrats’ scramble to retake Congress. The most consequential campaign right now is in Michigan — but Obama, Harris and especially Coates are clearly projecting onto the presidential contest in 2028. In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is running a must-win race against his Republican challenger, former Congressman Mike Rogers. The key obstacle for El-Sayed is not Blacks — but Jews, who could very likely abandon Michigan Democrats owing to the Egyptian-American physician’s impossible-to-ignore antisemitic outbursts and alignment with Islamists. Michigan’s Jewish vote totals around 130,000, but in this Ozempic-thin race, every ballot will matter. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER And so enter Harris and Obama. There are far more Blacks in Michigan than Jews, but the former, like the latter, are beginning to tilt rightward. Black support for El-Sayed is far lower than it needs to be, with African Americans complaining they feel both overlooked by his campaign, as well as turned off by his over-emphasis on Israel, Gaza and Palestinian issues. As one Black Michigander summed up in a recent clever Rogers ad, "El-Sayed cares more about the West Bank than West Detroit." Harris was in Michigan in late September to campaign with El-Sayed and rally Black support. At least that was the plan. Instead, both Democrats devolved into displays of characteristic Kamala "word salad" that clearly did more harm than good. Now Obama will parachute into Detroit this weekend to mop up Harris’ mess, just as new ties emerge between El-Sayed's family and Egypt’s extremist Muslim Brotherhood. Obama may think he’s smart to drop Israel and Palestine into this already combustive mix, but the #gazamaxxing — by him, Harris and Coates — reveals more about their intractable out-of-touchness than actual Black concern for the Middle East. Indeed, according to the Fox News poll, African Americans were the racial group most likely to say the U.S. isn't supportive enough of Israel when asked the question along with White and Hispanic voters. That number was 25% compared with 19% for Hispanic voters and 15% for White voters. African American voters were also the least likely of the three groups to agree that America was too supportive of Israel, with 40% disagreeing as compared to White voters at 44% and Hispanic voters at 56%. The stat stands sharply against the ubiquitous notion that African Americans — owing to supposed shared experiences of injustice and oppression — organically align with the Palestinian experience. Take it from someone who’s both African American and Jewish American, such "intersectional" overreach is little more than a myth — Blacks and Palestinians have nothing in common. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Our Civil Rights struggle — the one my own father fought to help desegregate his South Texas school — succeeded precisely because of its commitment to nonviolence. As for the Palestinians, violence — whether in Gaza, Israel, the streets of New York and now most spectacularly, along the grand boulevards of Paris — is the only thing their "liberation" movement has ever known. Such statements are not Islamophobic — they’re simply facts. Obama and Harris know this — El-Sayed probably does too. But no matter identity and entitlement are what the Dems have always done best and none are more entitled than Harris, Obama and Coates. This is why all three chose to lean into Israel well beyond the critical eyes of the actual African-Americans they claim to care so much about — Obama and Harris, respectively, in Europe and Asia; the irrationally Israel-obsessed Coates fielding sycophantic, softball prompts from a fawning white host in New York. Masters at manipulating racial anxiety and white guilt, the trio were performing for white audiences too fearful of being canceled or called racist to offer any meaningful pushback. This is why their anti-Zionist screeds passed with scant consequence or criticism — because they landed, as intended, so far from Black ears. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ultimately, Kamala, Obama and Coates could have easily attacked Israel at a church or community event or in leading Black media outlets. But then they would have been jolted by the reality that African-Americans — now contending with outsized homicide numbers and roughly twice the unemployment figures of their white counterparts — have far more crucial concerns than chanting for a "Free Palestine."
news.summary: Obama and Harris used recent speeches abroad to focus on Israel and the Palestinians, while Black voters at home appear more concerned with the midterms than the Middle East.

news.title: Becerra's time in Washington: Steady rise with a bumpy final ascent
news.text: Xavier Becerra was dubbed a "rising star" before he even entered the halls of Congress. His June 1992 Democratic primary victory over Los Angeles school board member Leticia Quezada in California’s 30th Congressional District earned the 34-year-old candidate that description in The Times. When the boyish, affable congressman became the first Latino lawmaker appointed to the powerful House Ways and Means Committee in his second term, national outlets took notice. Thirty years later, in the final weeks of his gubernatorial race with Republican Steve Hilton, Becerra now finds himself poised to lead the most populous state in the country. An examination of Becerra’s more than 25 years in Washington shows a politician who was skilled at building important alliances and amassing power on Capitol Hill, but had some stumbles along the way and faced criticism for his performance in his highest profile role. Becerra built his reputation as a diligent consensus-builder — a workhorse rather than a show horse, to use an analogy favored by political scientists — but also revealed himself to be an ambitious political operator in key moments. "He's an affable person who's not afraid to pull out a knife in politics while smiling," said Christian Grose, a political science professor at USC. Becerra's campaign declined to comment on his time in Washington. Becerra’s origin story traces back to his youth in Sacramento, and a moment when a high school friend was about to throw out a blank, unused application to Stanford University. The elite university was only 125 miles away, but it might as well have been across the ocean from the working-class world Becerra was raised in. Still, he applied. Becerra — whose parents spent their early years in Mexico — became the first in his family to graduate from college when he earned a degree from Stanford in 1980. He earned a law degree there four years later, and it was at Stanford that he met his wife, Carolyn Reyes, who became a physician. After living in Boston while Reyes attended Harvard Medical School, Becerra moved to Los Angeles to work for state Sen. Art Torres. Within a few years he was tapped by Henry Lozano, then chief of staff to trailblazing Latino Rep. Edward Roybal, to run for state Assembly in 1990; and then, two years later, to succeed Roybal, who was retiring after 30 years in Congress. Roybal endorsed Becerra, whose victory in the heavily Latino district that included Central and Eastside Los Angeles communities, was seen as a passing of the torch to the next generation. Frank Villalobos, the founder and president of Barrio Architects, was among the leaders in East L.A. who encouraged Becerra to run for political office, and he said he was impressed early on by Becerra's genuine commitment to the community and his ability to unite the area's sometimes divided political factions. "I thought if we kept this going, someday he'll become the governor," Villalobos said. Becerra was part of a wave of young Latino lawmakers entering Congress, and his growing power within Democratic ranks helped him escape Roybal's long shadow. Soon after Becerra's barrier-breaking appointment to the Ways and Means Committee — which writes tax legislation — Becerra became chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, a position he held from 1997 to 1999. He put his growing stature to the test a few years later when he decided to enter the L.A. mayor’s race in 2001. It didn’t go well. Former state Assembly Speaker Antonio Villaraigosa was also running, and Becerra — who had slept on Villaraigosa’s couch when he first ran for Congress — faced criticism for potentially splitting the Latino vote. Becerra performed poorly, winning only 6% of the vote in the Democratic primary. His nice-guy reputation took a hit when his campaign was found to have been behind automated phone calls attacking Villaraigosa by a woman who falsely gave the impression that she was county Supervisor Gloria Molina, whose endorsement had been crucial in Becerra's first run for Congress. Becerra also faced criticism for his role in contacting White House staffers as part of an effort to push for the release of convicted L.A. cocaine dealer Carlos Vignali, whose father was a political contributor to Becerra. Vignali's sentence was commuted by President Clinton on his last day in office; Becerra acknowledged calling the White House several times to discuss the possibility of Vignali's release. Villaraigosa also wrote a letter on Vignali's behalf. Becerra told The Times in 2001 that he wasn't lobbying for Vignali's release, but merely asking White House officials to review the details of the conviction on behalf of the family. "If I was going to try to put pressure on, I would have tried to call the president," Becerra said at the time. Villaraigosa fared better than Becerra but ultimately lost the 2001 election to City Atty. James Hahn, then rebounded to win the first of two terms as mayor in 2005. Becerra got the better of Villaraigosa in their rematch this year in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, and won Villaraigosa’s support after. "We've been friends a long time and, yes, we've been adversaries as well, but most of the time we've been friends,” Villaraigosa told The Times. “He's got the experience and the wherewithal to lead this state.” As for Becerra as a house guest during his first run for Congress? “He makes his bed. He was neat,” said Villaraigosa. “He was pretty inconspicuous.” After his mayoral defeat, Becerra’s focus returned to Washington, where an alliance with another powerful Californian was a boon to his career on Capitol Hill. Becerra was a close ally of former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-San Francisco), serving as assistant to the speaker from 2007 to 2009. John Lawrence, Pelosi's former chief of staff, said that Becerra's standing within the California delegation and particularly among Latino lawmakers was a big part of his appeal. "Speaker Pelosi had set a goal of elevating minorities and women who had historically been excluded from leadership," he said. Their relationship took a hit after Becerra told progressive lawmakers in 2009 that he believed party leadership gave up too easily on including a public option in the Affordable Care Act, which was signed into law the following year. "I understand I have tire tracks on my back because Xavier threw me under the bus,” Pelosi said during a Democratic Party leadership meeting in 2009, Politico reported. And Pelosi would later question Becerra's appointment in 2021 to be secretary of Health and Human Services. She has not endorsed Becerra in the gubernatorial race. But any bad blood between the two didn't stop Becerra from continuing to advance within the party ranks. He became chair of the House Democratic Caucus in 2012, leading weekly meetings of all Democrats in the House and uniting the party’s members. Former Wisconsin Democratic Rep. Ron Kind said Becerra was an excellent listener and skilled at building consensus. “He could get in the room with anyone and find common ground,” Kind said. Becerra joined several high-stakes negotiations, notably a 2013 bipartisan effort to pass comprehensive immigration reform, in the wake of the “Gang of Eight” deal struck in the Senate. John Yarmuth, a Democratic congressman from Kentucky who was also part of the House negotiation, said Becerra was “an amazing positive force” in the process. “I think he, more than anyone else, was focused on fixing the problem,” Yarmuth said. The group was able to achieve a compromise, but it never saw the light of day. Then-House Speaker John Boehner, an Ohio Republican, later blamed then-President Obama, whom he accused of “poisoning the well” on an immigration compromise. Yarmuth said Republicans were spooked about potential blowback. Several potential off-ramps appeared during Becerra’s time in Washington. He was considered by Obama for U.S. trade representative in 2008, but Becerra declined the offer. After flirting with the idea of running for outgoing U.S. Sen. Barbara Boxer’s seat, Becerra declined to enter the race, ultimately won by then-California Atty. Gen. Kamala Harris. He was briefly floated as a potential running mate for Hillary Clinton in the 2016 presidential election, but that didn’t materialize either. In late 2016, Becerra found himself at a crossroads. After more than a decade on the Ways and Means Committee, he faced the possibility of becoming the top Democrat on the committee and had the endorsement of the outgoing top Democrat, Rep. Sander Levin of Michigan. But Harris’ victory in the 2016 Senate race created a vacancy for state attorney general. Becerra decided to return home to Sacramento to take the role and spent the next four years as the state’s top law enforcement official, serving as "defender-in-chief" of the state, as USC's Grose put it, against the Trump administration. Becerra returned to Washington in 2021 for a second act that would prove to be far more controversial than his first. Despite having no background in healthcare, Becerra was nominated to be the secretary of Health and Human Services and confirmed, over significant opposition by Republicans. He took the reins of the healthcare agency as the country was still grappling with the COVID-19 pandemic and struggled to establish a clear role for himself in a response effort that was centered in the White House. In his first year in office, he was called out by reporters for failing to hold regular press briefings. And he faced criticism when health officials under his purview offered contradictory information in late 2021 about reduced quarantine requirements for people testing positive for COVID-19. He continued to face criticism for the disappearance of thousands of unaccompanied migrant children who were supposed to be monitored by the agency’s Office of Refugee Resettlement after entering the country. And Becerra's chief of staff at Health and Human Services and longtime advisor, Sean McCluskie, pleaded guilty last year to participating in a scheme to use campaign funds from a dormant Becerra state political committee to pay for McCluskie's frequent travel between Washington and California. Dana Williamson, a longtime political consultant for Becerra and former chief of staff to Gov. Gavin Newsom, pleaded guilty earlier this year for her role in the scheme. McCluskie and Williamson are scheduled to be sentenced in December. Neither Becerra nor Newsom were accused of wrongdoing. Democratic operative Xochitl Hinojosa, who served as the spokesperson for the Department of Justice in the Biden administration, earlier this year offered a blunt assessment of Becerra’s performance. “He was not effective in government, and I think that a lot of people in the Biden administration are talking about this because they realize that he was not an effective HHS secretary,” Hinojosa said on CNN in May. While other members of the Biden administration have defended Becerra’s performance, his time at the helm highlighted an issue that even allies concede has bedeviled Becerra in the past, his tendency to sometimes recede into the background. Loretta Sanchez, a former Democratic congresswoman from Orange County who credits Becerra with encouraging her to run for Congress, put it simply. “Will Xavier be bold?” she said. “I hope he takes those bold moves, because California needs it.”
news.summary: In his more than 25 years in Washington, Xavier Becerra built important alliances and amassed power on Capitol Hill, but had some stumbles along the way.
news.author: Ben Wieder

news.title: The Sununu Dynasty Faces Biggest Test in New Hampshire Senate Race
news.text: New Hampshire’s Senate race will test the power of the Sununu name as former Senator John Sununu hopes to boost Republicans in midterm elections that will likely prove complicated for the GOP. Sununu is seeking a comeback in the Granite State against Democratic Representative Chris Pappas to replace retiring Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen. New Hampshire narrowly backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, and the state has generally leaned toward Democrats in statewide elections, so Pappas has been viewed as a favorite. But some polls have pointed to a closer-than-expected race. The Sununu family is an institution in New Hampshire. In addition to the former senator, who held the seat from 2003 to 2009, his father, John H. Sununu, served as governor in the 1980s, and his brother Chris Sununu was governor from 2017 to 2025. But this election could test the power of the Sununu name. His brother withstood tough electoral environments for the GOP in 2018 and 2020. But this race is different. Trump is less popular than ever in the polls, and federal races are generally more partisan than governor’s races. The Sununu name gives the former senator a modest advantage over a generic Republican in New Hampshire, Andrew Smith, director of the University of New Hampshire Survey Center, told Newsweek. But he said national issues like the economy are likely to weigh heavier for voters than the popularity of the political dynasty. “The way I look at it is that Sununu’s name recognition probably gives him about a 3 percentage point advantage over a generic Republican running,” he said. “He’s been in office so he can point to him being an experienced person to be able to step into this race. Pappas is generally well known, but not seen as somebody who is on the cutting edge of the Democratic Party.” The Sununu family has had “some really strong people” running and serving in office, Neil Levesque, the executive director of the New Hampshire Institute of Politics, told Newsweek. Sununu’s ability to localize the election, knowing the issues important to New Hampshire voters and running strong ads has put him in a better position than would be expected in this environment, he said, noting that he still wouldn’t classify the race as close. Pappas, he noted, has also been on the ballot several times in his district—which comprises half of the state’s population—and comes from a well-known family. His family owns the Manchester restaurant Puritan Backroom, which has been credited with inventing chicken tenders. “The real name that people do know is Donald Trump, and that’s really what is motivating a lot of voters at this point,” he said. “Although Trump’s name is not on the ballot, and you have Sununu and Pappas with their own strong name recognition and branding, Trump is the motivating factor here in midterm elections.” Sununu sought to put some distance between himself and Trump in a new ad. “The way Chris Pappas tells it, I’m President Trump’s long-lost son. I’ve never even met the man. When the president’s policies are bad for New Hampshire, I’ll oppose them, just like I’ve opposed the war in Iran and the trade war with Canada,” he said. Newsweek reached out to the Pappas and Sununu campaigns for comment via email. How the Sununu Family Became Political Institution in New Hampshire John H. Sununu’s 1982 victory in the gubernatorial race began a political dynasty that would span decades in New Hampshire. He served in that role until 1989, and later served as the chief of staff to then President George H. W. Bush from 1989 to 1991. Having that prominent of a position “solidified” the Sununu family as important in New Hampshire politics, said Smith. Only a few years later, his son John E. Sununu would be elected to Congress, representing New Hampshire’s 1st District. At that time, the state still leaned Republican but was starting to shift, Smith said, noting that his father’s connections helped him early in the political career. He won the Senate race in 2002 and served one term before losing to Shaheen, then the former governor, in a difficult year for the GOP. The Sununu family was not absent from state government for long—Chris Sununu was elected to the New Hampshire Executive Council in 2010 and governor in 2016, even as former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton edged out President Donald Trump in the state on the same ballot. He won reelection in tough years for Republicans, including 2018, the last time there was a “blue wave” year during Trump’s first term, and 2020, when former President Joe Biden carried the state by just over 7 points. Having that name recognition helped him in those races, Smith said. But he did not seek reelection in 2024. This year, it is the brother and former senator, John E. Sununu, who is seeking to return to office, nearly two decades after his loss to Shaheen. Can John Sununu Defy Political Gravity? A lot has changed in the state since Sununu last ran for office. “About half of the people in the state weren’t eligible to vote or didn’t live in the state back when he ran for office last time,” said Smith. Sununu will have to defy political headwinds to defeat Pappas in this year’s midterm. In a state that has backed Democrats at the federal level in recent cycles, Pappas is seen as having an advantage due to the overall national environment. A flurry of polls in late August and early September showed a tight race, giving Republicans hope that Sununu could overcome the national environment and flip the seat. A University of New Hampshire poll of 1,846 likely voters from August 20 to 24 showed Sununu up 2 points, 45 percent to 43 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.3 percentage points. A handful of GOP internal polls also showed a tight race. The Cook Political Report temporarily shifted the race to the toss-up category in mid-September. But polling has shifted in Pappas’ favor. The latest UNH poll, conducted from September 17 to 21, gave Pappas an 8-point lead, 50 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 1,392 likely voters and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Another poll from The New York Times and Siena University gave Pappas a 5-point lead, 50 percent to 45 percent, among 613 likely voters from September 15 to 22. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. The Senate race “definitely leans Democratic,” Smith said. “It would be difficult for Sununu to pull this one out,” he said. “It’s likely to be a very good year for Democrats, both here and across the country.” GOP’s Elusive Swing State With an Independent Streak At the federal level, New Hampshire has emerged as an elusive state for Republicans. The Granite State regularly elects Republican governors, but it has continued to lean Democratic in federal races. It last voted for a Republican president in 2000. Democrats have also performed strongly in recent U.S. Senate races, winning every contest in the state since 2016. The state is generally seen as politically moderate with a libertarian streak, and it has backed politicians from both parties over the years. In 2024, the state narrowly went to Harris, 50.7 percent to 47.9 percent. But it gave President Joe Biden a wider victory in 2020, backing him by 7 points. In 2016, it was one of the country's closest races, backing former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by less than half a percentage point. New Hampshire’s southern and central region is fairly dense around cities like Manchester, Concord, Portsmouth, Dover and Nashua. Many of those cities lean Democratic, though not always overwhelmingly, while Republicans perform strongly in many smaller towns and communities. Undeclared voters are the largest voter group in New Hampshire. As of September 18, 307,254 New Hampshirites were not registered with either party, according to the Secretary of State’s office. There were 298,965 registered Republicans and 255,943 registered Democrats. New England Backs Political Dynasties in High Profile Contests Political dynasties have been having a strong year in New England. Also in New Hampshire, Senator Shaheen’s daughter, Stefany Shaheen, won the Democratic primary to succeed Pappas in the House. The Cook Political Report considers the race to be Likely Democratic. In neighboring Maine, Hannah Pingree, the daughter of Representative Chellie Pingree, won the Democratic primary in the state’s gubernatorial race. She defeated Angus King III, the son of Senator Angus King, among several other Democrats, to win the nomination. Pingree is seen as the favorite to win the general election. Meanwhile, in Rhode Island, Helena Foulkes, the niece of former Senator Chris Dodd, defeated incumbent Governor Dan McKee in the Democratic primary and is also seen as the favorite to win in November.

news.title: Language, Please!
news.text: If President Donald Trump had a pet parrot, it wouldn’t pick up as many obscenities as that of its 19th-century predecessor, President Andrew Jackson’s feathered friend “Poll.” Trump has nothing on his favorite president (other than himself) when it comes to cussing. Newsweek readers were tetchy about the latest foul-mouthed bout from Trump, who was speaking at a midterm rally at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio, this month. “Just get out and vote,” he said. “If you do...we’re going to win big! And we’re going to shove it up their ass, OK.” But the seventh president was reportedly much worse than the 47th when it comes to potty talk. Jackson’s parrot picked up so much foul language, it was said that the bird had to be removed from the house at Jackson’s funeral in 1845. Meanwhile, Democrats and the left are confusing Trump’s language with concerns about the “dignity of office” (two very different things); and swearing has become a cheat code for politicians to suggest they are not really politicians at all. “Such a fine example of how a POTUS should act and talk,” said one comment on the report of Trump in Ohio. “Thirty years ago Christians were appalled by [President] Bill Clinton’s behavior,” said another. “Amazing how much they have lowered the bar on morals and family values.” “MAGA likes it, yet decent Americans are turned off—and embarrassed—by such UNpresidential displays,” summed up the general tone of disapproval. Classic confirmation bias. If you wanted to argue that Trump has demeaned his office, there is no shortage of supporting material. But presidents swearing? If anything, Trump is not even in the top division. The majority of readers who voted on the article’s fairness (46 percent) said it “leans right” (12 percent said “leans left”), which suggests only an outright condemnation would have been enough to satisfy those who hate him. But President Joe Biden was caught open mic saying the Affordable Care Act signing was “a big f***ing deal” in 2010, and in 2022 he called a Fox News reporter a “stupid son of a b****.” President Richard Nixon and President Lyndon B. Johnson were famously sweary in private, and LBJ was caught telling the Greek ambassador “f*** your parliament” in 1964. Even the saintly President Jimmy Carter said, of Senator Ted Kennedy, he would “whip his ass” if he ran against him in 1980. More recently, bad language has become a verbal trick politicians use to show us they are “real” and “authentic” in a culture where nobody wants to be associated with the establishment, imagined or otherwise. Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth (who has somehow fallen into office straight from a 1980s teen comedy in which he played the school jerk) love to portray themselves as insurgents, hence the “sh**” here and “ass” there, but Democrats are willing to stress their normalcy too, with cursing being a shortcut to connect with disaffected voters. Last October, former Vice President Kamala Harris condemned her political opponents by saying “these mother******* are crazy.” A month later, Senator Chuck Schumer said the Trump administration cannot “f*** around” over the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files. All very edgy. The last bad word falls to that paragon of dignity, President George W. Bush. During the 2000 election campaign, he was overheard calling a journalist a “major-league asshole.” W. later expressed “regret” at the remark. How unpresidential.
news.summary: Politicians are dropping profanities left and right. History tells us it's nothing new for a president.

news.title: Fiscal strength doesn't guarantee public goods delivery, US study finds
news.text:
New York/DNA - A newly released study of US state government performance found strong partisan and regional patterns within three pillars of governance: democratic accountability, state capacity and public goods provision. Yet, the US states’ outcomes differ in important ways from international comparisons, as the three governance dimensions show limited correlation, the researchers found. 

The report, “The Governance Performance of the Fifty States: The U.S. Berggruen Governance Index”, applies the research team’s “governance triangle” from past global country rankings to the 50 US states. The report has now been presented to the public at Columbia University in New York.

“Unlike in the Berggruen Governance Index’s cross-national comparisons, where the three dimensions are broadly correlated, in the 50 U.S. states they often run counter to each other,” the authors conclude. “This may seem counterintuitive, as one might expect a well-governed state to finish high on all three and a poorly governed one to place low across all three.”

The report concluded that state capacity and public goods provision are “essentially uncorrelated.” Massachusetts, which has among the highest per capita incomes, was third in public goods but 49th in state capacity. Mining and agriculture-dependent Wyoming was 36th in public goods provision but No. 1 in state capacity.

 Public goods provision, which combines quality-of-life metrics such as health and educational outcomes with infrastructure and quasi-public goods that are often delivered by the private sector, saw four of the top five from the Northeast, while the bottom seven were in the South. All but one of the top 16 states were won by Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the 2024 US presidential election. Nineteen of the bottom 20 went to Donald Trump.
 Democratic accountability measures election procedures, which vary widely among states, along with scores for civil society activity and government openness. These include among others lobbying disclosures and state auditor independence. The top 12 states were a geographical mix of the West, Northeast and Midwest. Nine of that dozen voted for Harris, though the state with the highest score was reliably Republican Montana. The 10 lowest-ranked states were all Southern, and the bottom 20 were all won by Trump in 2024.
 State capacity foremost indicates debt levels, along with budget processes and effective welfare-state delivery such as unemployment insurance. The top-ranked states were geographically diversified, but no Northeastern state was among the top 12. All major regions were represented in the bottom 10, including notoriously debt-laden Rhode Island, Illinois, Connecticut and New Jersey.

The three components produce four state groupings identified by the authors:

 14 fiscally sound and delivering states, which are half Republican and half Democratic and swing states, based on the 2024 presidential race.
 16 strained but delivering states, which are mostly Democratic.
 Nine fiscally strong but poorly served states, almost entirely Republican.
 11 low performing states, including only one Democratic state.

The report was written by principal investigator Helmut K. Anheier with co-authors Joseph C. Saraceno and Edward L. Knudsen, all of the UCLA Luskin School of Public Affairs, and produced as a collaboration of the Luskin School with the Berlin-based Hertie School, supported by the Berggruen Institute, a Los Angeles think tank.

During a panel discussion held with the release of the report at Columbia University, economic historian Adam Tooze focused on the states with poor scores for provision of public goods. He pointed out that for many public goods that in Europe are assumed to be state-led, such as health care, education and utilities, in the US the private sector has a greater role. 

“If you look at all of the states which are underperforming, it's the South, and the variable that's operating here is race,” said Tooze, a Columbia professor. “The reason why these states don't have large-scale public services is that white people who are richer don't want to pay taxes to redistribute income to black people. And it's not a secret; it's the logic of American politics.”

Among the 11 low performing states, the very worst performers are in the South: Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Kentucky.

Joseph C. Saraceno said that the 14 states classified in the report as fiscally sound and delivering “provide a moderate level of public goods while also having state capacity, or this measure of fiscal room that they find to be comfortable, or have a rainy day fund as needed.”

The group of fiscally strong, poorly served states have strong balance sheets but little to show for it in quality of life. Arkansas, for example, ranks seventh in state capacity but 46th in public goods provision. Tooze said those states have better fiscal resilience and “rank high on their capacity score because basically they've never done anything. So unsurprisingly, when push comes to shove, they could do something if one supposed they had politics that would allow them to.”

Edward Knudsen, another researcher who worked on the previous global versions of the Berggruen Governance Index, pointed out that the strained but delivering states are heavily traditionally Democratic Party states that also score higher for democratic accountability. “In a lot of the Democratic leaning states, you have more ability for the population to demand public goods. They in turn are able to receive them. That places this fiscal stress,” Knudsen said.

The full report “The Governance Performance of the Fifty States: The U.S. Berggruen Governance Index” can be downloaded here: https://ucla.app.box.com/s/hcruhr43fyhfw0uondid2e6fviqopmww

news.title: Senate Democrats Launch First Ad In Mississippi As Their Midterm Optimism Spreads In The South
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democrats’ top campaign spending group is wading into Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race for the first time this year, an aggressive move in a deep-red state that signals a party on the offensive as Republicans look to protect a slim majority.

The Senate Majority PAC, aligned with Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, will spend $1.2 million on a new television advertisement to boost Scott Colom, a district attorney, in his campaign against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. The ad, first disclosed to The Associated Press, is set to start Wednesday and run through Election Day.

“Senate Majority PAC has been watching this race closely, and it is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” group spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement.

With just two weeks to go in the race, it’s unclear what impact the ad will have in a matchup that’s been set since Colom won a March primary. Still, it’s a substantial investment in a race that’s seen only about $8 million in total spending, with Colom outspending Hyde-Smith nearly $4.6 million to $3.2 million, according to AdImpact.

Jake Monssen, campaign manager for Hyde-Smith, noted that the spending was coming late in the race.

“Team Cindy is confident that voters will reject this radical agenda at the ballot box on November 3rd,” he said.

Democrats believe Hyde-Smith is vulnerable

Hyde-Smith, first appointed and then elected in 2018, is running for reelection in a state Republicans have long dominated. In the 2024 presidential race, Republican Donald Trump won Mississippi by nearly 23 percentage points over Democrat Kamala Harris, and a Democrat hasn’t won a Senate race in the state since 1982.

However, some Democrats believe Hyde-Smith is vulnerable, and she underperformed Trump by 6 percentage points in 2020, the year he lost his White House reelection bid to Democrat Joe Biden.

The television ad touts Colom’s time as district attorney, while labeling Hyde-Smith a “do-nothing” senator.

“A decade in power, Hyde-Smith hasn’t passed one piece of legislation, but she did vote to kick people off Medicaid,” a narrator says in the ad, which will run on television stations statewide alongside a digital campaign.

Harris and other high-profile Democrats have raced to campaign with Colom

Colom’s campaign manager, Gerard Henderson, said that the contest against an incumbent senator is competitive because “thousands of Mississippians volunteered and chipped in.”

“We clearly have the resources and momentum to win,” Henderson said in a statement.

Colom has raised Democratic hopes in a year when electoral winds are at their backs. Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock was the latest high-profile Democrat to campaign with Colom last week, and Harris, who was Biden’s vice president, is set to rally with Colom on Thursday.

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and were expected to face a friendlier map this year with fewer seats to defend. But high costs and gas prices amid an unpopular war in Iran under a Republican president have made Democrats optimistic, with the Senate Majority PAC spending its final weeks investing in conservative territory. It’s already announced spending in Kansas, where megachurch pastor and Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton is trying to unseat Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.

Colom would be his state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, the 12-year period after the U.S. Civil War when the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments were adopted.

Some Democrats have criticized national groups for not spending more in Southern states like Mississippi.

“I worry, to be very honest, that Democrats are missing a real opportunity to invest in a serious and sustained way in the South,” Warnock said Sunday on NBC’s ”Meet the Press.”

news.title: Barbara Bush openly donates cash to Democrat James Talarico
news.text:
James Talarico, the Democratic state representative locked in a tight, high-profile race for U.S. Senate in Texas, is getting some support from the daughter of a former Republican President.

Barbara Bush, the 44-year-old daughter of George W. and Laura Bush, donated to Lone Star Rising, a political action committee supporting Talarico, Federal Election Commission records show. Campaign finance records indicate a $2,500 contribution from Bush on Sept. 23.

While Bush’s gift is small potatoes amid the hundreds of millions that have poured into Talarico’s campaign, political lawyer Andrew Cates told Houston Public Media, which broke the news on Oct. 16, that it nonetheless could hold symbolic value.

"It’s not like Elon Musk money, obviously," he said, "but it is it is interesting and maybe potentially a little bit telling on where the center GOP establishment is leaning and where they feel like the race is headed."

Cates, a campaign finance expert, noted that Bush didn’t try to keep her contribution under the radar.

"I would imagine that somebody in such a prominent political family, if she wanted to ensure that her contribution was anonymous or not visible, that any number of lawyers that they probably have at their disposal could have told her how," he said.

The Bush family did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It’s not the first time the former president’s daughter has tilted across party lines. In 2024, Bush campaigned in Pennsylvania for Vice President and Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

Bush, the twin sister of Jenna Hager Bush, is currently senior vice president of social impact and inclusion for the National Basketball Association. She's supported abortion and reproductive rights, addressing a rally for Planned Parenthood in 2017. In 2010, she told People magazine she didn’t identify with either party.

She’s also co-founder of Global Health Corps (GHC), an organization mobilizing young leaders to address critical health issues. 

Her namesake and late grandmother, former first lady Barbara Bush, told USA TODAY in an interview months before her death in 2018 she "probably" would not still consider herself a Republican. The prominent GOP family matriarch blamed President Donald Trump for making the party unrecognizable to her.

According to Susan Page’s biography The Matriarch, Barbara Bush wrote in her 1990 private diaries that Donald Trump was greedy, selfish, and ugly.

Polls generally show Talarico and his Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, statistically tied or indicate Talarico has a slight edge.

news.title: Kansas Dem Adam Hamilton Lamented Trump’s Reversal of Biden Transgender Orders: ‘Tears and Brokenness’
news.text:
Kansas Democrat Senate nominee Adam Hamilton read descriptions of four executive orders issued under former President Joe Biden concerning gender identity and LGBTQ protections to his congregation during a January 2025 sermon, saying the thought of losing those protections was painful for people in the LGBTQ community.

Hamilton, the founding and senior pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, made the remarks in a January 2025 message titled A Message to President Trump, following Trump’s return to the White House.

The pastor, who is challenging incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS) in Kansas’s U.S. Senate race, referenced a message he had received that morning from a member of his congregation.

“And somebody sent me this morning, one of our gay members sent me this morning, the executive orders that were rescinded yesterday,” Hamilton said. “And, you know, people clapped and cheered about these executive orders being rescinded. These were executive orders from the Biden Administration, from 2021. Let me just read a couple of them to you.”

“Executive Order 14021, guaranteeing an educational environment free from discrimination based on sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. That’s been rescinded,” Hamilton said.

“Executive Order 14004, enabling all qualified Americans to serve their country in uniform regardless of gender identity. That’s been rescinded,” he continued.

“Executive Order 13988, preventing and combating discrimination on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation. That has been rescinded. Executive Order 14075 advancing equality for LGBTQI+ individuals. That’s been rescinded,” Hamilton said.

After listing the orders, Hamilton stated, “For people who find themselves in this community, the thought that the rights that they had — basic fundamental protections that they had — have been rescinded is painful,” Hamilton said. “It leads to tears and brokenness.”

He then addressed how the Church of the Resurrection would respond.

“We’re going to be a safe place for people, where you don’t have to be afraid,” Hamilton said. “This is a safe place for you.”

One of the orders Hamilton referenced, Executive Order 13988, titled Preventing and Combating Discrimination on the Basis of Gender Identity or Sexual Orientation, was issued by Biden on January 20, 2021. The directive established the administration’s nondiscrimination policy concerning gender identity and sexual orientation, including protections affecting education, employment, healthcare, and housing. It stated that “Children should be able to learn without worrying about whether they will be denied access to the restroom, the locker room, or school sports,” and called for equal treatment under the law regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation.

In a February 2021 analysis, Sarah Parshall Perry of the Heritage Foundation argued that while the order did not explicitly link federal funding to transgender-identifying athletes’ participation in girls’ and women’s sports, schools could still face financial consequences. She wrote that refusing to allow biological males who identify as women to compete on female sports teams or receive athletic scholarships could, under the Biden administration’s interpretation of Title IX, “constitute a violation of Title IX, thereby disqualifying said institution from receiving certain federal funds.”

Executive Order 13988 also influenced federal housing policy. On April 27, 2021, the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) withdrew a proposed Trump administration rule that would have weakened protections for transgender individuals seeking access to federally funded shelters and housing programs. The decision also had implications for domestic violence shelters serving women. HUD cited Executive Order 13988 and Executive Order 13985, titled Advancing Racial Equity and Support for Underserved Communities Through the Federal Government, in explaining the withdrawal. The decision preserved the department’s 2016 Equal Access Rule, which was designed to ensure that “all individuals — regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity, or marital status — had equal access to HUD-funded and HUD-insured housing and related programs.”

news.title: Kamala Harris' stunning pixie cut has to be seen to be believed
news.text:
Kamala Harris, the former Democratic nominee for President of the United States, is known for her glossy and bouncy haircut, which she has previously revealed she manages with a round brush and silk presses. 

The "Presidential" look inspired countless women to rush to their stylists for a similar look and hundreds of thousands of tutorials on TiKTok, and has become as famous for the politicians as the Rachel did for Jennifer Aniston in the 1990s.

But Kamala hasn't always had long, luscious locks – and in fact, had a wildly different hairstyle in the 1980s when in college.

The budding activist spent much of her childhood wearing her hair in braids, a decision made by her mother.

"I wanted to wear it out, and it's so funny because I would go to school, and you know, she would have put it in the two braids, and then as soon as I got to school, I would take the braids out," she said in 2024 as she ran for President, admitting she would then rebraid her hair before arriving home.

That rebellious attitude came to fruition when she enrolled at Howard University in 1982 and went for the ultimate change – a pixie cut.

The classic '80s look included a short back and curly sides, and she told Cocoa Butter the decision was made simply because it was "easy."

"Instead of having, you know, to deal with the amount of time that it takes to do your own hair or get it done, which I really couldn't afford to do, it just was easy when I was in college. I just didn't want to have to put that kind of time into worrying about my hair," she said.

Kamala studied political science and economics at the HBCU and also joined her sorority; it was during rush week the picture above was taken.

"So, this is a photograph [from] when I was joining my sorority during a particularly active week in front of Rankin Chapel, that's where we are here, where we would go every Sunday for service," she said in a video, which you can watch below.

Now in her 60s, Kamala remains true to the blowout she is known for – a medium-length, layered blowout with soft waves and flipped ends. She has experimented with color, adding honey-blonde highlights in 2024.

She doesn't use a curling iron, she told Keke Palmer in 2023, admitting it is "too much heat."

Typical silk presses, according to Essence, often use heat as high as 450 degrees, so instead, Kamala uses a round boar-bristle brush to blow out her hair and avoid heat damage. "It takes a lot of heat [for a silk press], but it's just too much to do that and [a hot tool]," said Kamala.

news.title: Rogers says inroads with Black and Jewish voters will help him beat El-Sayed
news.text:
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers said he's been successful reaching out to traditional Democratic constituencies wary of his progressive opponent Abdul El-Sayed and tried to distance himself from President Donald Trump over tariffs and the economy in an interview with ABC News Live that airs Tuesday. 

Rogers is locked in a critical race for Michigan's open Senate seat that could determine control of the Senate in the next Congress.

A Fox News poll conducted in late September found the race essentially tied among likely voters, with El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 49%, well within the poll's margin of error.

Reaching out for crossover votes

Amidst concerns about turnout for El-Sayed among traditional Democratic constituencies like Black and Jewish voters, Rogers sees an opening for crossover votes.

He told ABC News Live anchor Linsey Davis that there's "an opportunity ... with Jewish Democrat voters, African Americans in Detroit and Pontiac and Brooklyn."

"We are going into what would normally be traditional Democrat coalitions, and we're getting such a great response. I think that's why we're going to win, and that's what's different," he said.

There is no polling to determine if Rogers is making gains in those coalitions.

Former President Barack Obama is headed to Detroit on Saturday to campaign with El-Sayed and former Vice President Kamala Harris appeared with him earlier in the campaign. 

Convincing Trump on new policy

When asked whether he agreed with the president's self assessment that he had done an "A++" job on the economy, Rogers did not directly answer the question, saying, "I am really worried. People are so frustrated. They're frustrated about prices. They're frustrated about inflation."

He argued that he would be able to effectively influence the president on economic policy.

"I'm going to be able to go in, sit down, talk to him about the things that work for Michigan."

Defending off-duty police officers as poll-watchers

Earlier this year, Rogers said "Let's put retired or off-duty police officers as our poll-watchers in Detroit. Go ahead, try to intimidate them."

He defended his statement to ABC News, saying, "I don't know how having a poll-watcher, which we've had for decades in the state, would discourage anyone from voting. I certainly would not encourage them to be discouraged in voting. I want it easy to vote, hard to cheat. That's it."

Rogers has previously called into doubt the results of his 2024 loss to Democratic Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin despite there being no evidence of wrongdoing or fraud in that race. 

Canadian tariffs are 'problematic'

In the closing weeks of the race, Rogers has made efforts to distance himself from Trump by breaking with a couple of his policies, including the Iran war and tariffs on goods from Canada, which shares a border with Michigan.

"This new round of Canadian tariffs are problematic for us here in the state," Rogers said, citing the two countries' "integrated" auto industries. 

"The Jeep Cherokee will go across the bridge between Canada and the United States about a dozen times before it's been built," Rogers told Davis.

"Let's get the Canadian deal done, or settled, or postponed, or let's negotiate, but don't put the tariffs on right now with all the other things, all the struggles that we have going on," he added.

According to a study by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, Michigan households are seeing an average additional cost of $5,600 due to tariffs since January 2025, the most of any state.

Defends connecting El-Sayed to terrorism

Rogers told CBS News last week to "look at the data -- it's pretty clear" when asked if he believed that El-Sayed was a terrorist.

Asked about that exchange and whether he believes El-Sayed is a terrorist, Rogers dodged the question, telling Davis, "It's not about how you pray, it is not about any of that. It is about how you think, it's about what your ideology is."

El-Sayed has denied any ties to terrorism and called those characterizations Islamophobic.

'Misconception' that he's a Washington insider

When asked what's the biggest misconception about him, Rogers said that it was that he was a "Washington insider," adding, "I've been out of Congress for 10 years in the private sector, working in the cybersecurity sector. I think that's the biggest misperception."

Rogers represented Michigan in the House for seven terms, including as chair of the House Intelligence Committee. 

Fair criticism 

When asked what the fairest criticism was of him, Rogers replied "I love my wife too much." 

His wife Kristi, joining the interview, said that when Rogers "says he's going to do something, he does it."
news.summary: He broke with Trump on some tariffs and said he’s “worried” about the economy.

news.text:

"Trump took to podcasts like The Joe Rogan Experience and This Past Weekend with Theo Von to boost his numbers among economically disaffected young white voters, while Kamala Harris failed to gain ground with them," reported The Daily Beast's Christopher Buchanan on Tuesday. "But amid his tumultuous term, Trump has had a contagious effect on most of the figures who propelled him back to the top."

Buchanan added, "Puck has revealed that individuals in the right-wing media sphere, including Tucker Carlson, Andrew Tate, and Joe Rogan, have all experienced double-digit drops in approval ratings since publicly backing Trump in 2024. War with Iran marked a turning point for the young men who helped to carry Trump to victory, devastating the economy and breaking key policy promises that distinguished it from the Harris campaign, a polling expert told Puck."

He also pointed out, "After feeling the blow of Trump’s newfound unpopularity, nearly all of the so-called Pod Bros have attempted to make like the voters and distance themselves from Trump."

Speaking with AlterNet in August, cult expert Dr. Steven Hassan explained how popular podcasters like Rogan help indoctrinate people into political cults like Trump's movement.

"It really comes down to what information sources they're relying on and who their network is that they identify with," Hassan explained to AlterNet. "So if they really love Joe Rogan, they're going to follow a lot of his views. And consequently, when he turns against Trump, Trump loses a lot of followers. What I'm trying to convey is that we're living in an age of digital manipulation that's never been seen before, with people's personal data being used to silo information — to drive them further left if they're already progressive-leaning, or further right if they're already Republican or conservative-leaning. And it's quite strategic in its use of algorithms. So it's not simply about looking at personality type, Matthew — the disposition of a person who becomes a Trump follower — but the social and information environment people are being subjected to."

Hassan also noted that, while Rogan had invited him on the program to discuss cults before Trump's presidency, he refused to speak with him when he wrote a book called "The Cult of Trump."

Rogan has indeed tried to separate himself from Trump recently, from accusing him of trying to rename Lake Ontario to distract from the war in Iran to outright saying in March that Trump "betrayed" his own voters because "he ran on, ‘No more wars,’ ‘End these stupid, senseless wars,’ and then we have one that we can’t even really clearly define why we did it.”

news.title: MAGA voters lament Trump as 'committed' allies abandon him: 'Embarrassed on a world stage'
news.text:
Two years ago, six White suburban mothers were among the more than 77 million Americans who voted to put President Donald Trump back in the White House. Now, they say they regret it. 

In a recent focus group convened by Navigator Research, a Democratic polling and public opinion firm, and shared exclusively with The 19th, the six Trump voters discussed their disappointment with his second term — and their mixed feelings about the upcoming midterm elections. Navigator shared the group with The 19th on the condition that the participants be referred to only by their first names to protect their privacy. 

Chrissy, a 44-year-old woman from Michigan, said that two years ago, she was “lazy” in basing her vote on political ads and discussions with others instead of her own research. 

Now, she’s committed to voting for candidates who will check Trump. 

“He’s pushed the country into an authoritarian playbook,” she said. “And if we don’t do something to stop it right now, it’s unlikely that there’ll be much left.” 

Trump is also losing women who were once among his most committed backers. 

“I was a die-hard supporter, but it's been a complete backstab since, pretty much, the storming of the Capitol for me,” said Kristen, a 39-year-old woman in Ohio. “That’s when my opinion really started changing about how he is as a leader.” 

Nicole, a 47-year-old in Texas, could relate. She believes Trump “might have his intentions in the right place,” but his second term hasn’t matched his campaign promises. She knows people struggling to afford groceries and turning to public assistance programs to make ends meet, and she thinks things “will get worse before they get better.” 

“I just feel we’re drowning, and it only started when Trump got in office,” she said. “I was fully, like she said, a die-hard fan of Trump. I mean, flag supporter, everything. Now I feel like I regret voting for him, I’ll just be honest.” 

Melissa Toufanian, a managing director at Navigator, said their research has found that 1 in 4 people who voted for Trump in 2024 now regret it. Moms are more likely to regret their votes than dads — and suburban women are a critical election demographic for both parties. 

While all the focus group participants have soured on Trump, they aren’t all sold on Democrats. Several expressed deep disillusionment with politics and doubted their votes could meaningfully change what they see as a broken status quo upheld by both political parties. 

“I do think in a lot of ways that our voice doesn't matter anymore,” said Gayle, a 47-year-old in Florida. “I think Congress sucks, honestly. I just think it sucks. I don't think that they're in it for the people. I think they're in it for themselves these days, and it's really on both sides.”

The cost of living consistently ranks as voters' top concern, and many Democratic candidates are putting affordability front and center in their campaigns. Polling from The 19th and YouGov found that women are more worried than men about paying for groceries, healthcare, housing and retirement. 

Even women who weren’t as personally affected by rising prices saw the war in Iran and the resulting increase in gas and fuel prices as a clear about-face from Trump’s 2024 campaign promises to lower costs. 

“I’m not struggling, but so many people are,” said Denise, a 49-year-old woman from Ohio. “I’m repulsed about the tariffs that we’ve put on our neighbor in Canada, the war, basically picking on other countries and just starting a war for no reason.” 

Of the entire group, Gayle had the most positive assessment of Trump’s second term and the economy. But she said she regretted voting for him because of the war in Iran, which “really messed things up.”

“If you're looking at the gas prices versus if I'm going to see a nuclear bomb happen, I'm more concerned with my gas prices than I am with the nuclear bomb, to be honest,” she said. 

And it wasn’t just the economy that made the women in the focus group turn against Trump. 

Denise pointed to Trump “taking down history because he's a narcissist” in tearing down the East Wing of the White House to build a new ballroom.

“It just … that disgusts me,” she said. “He had no right to do that, and that’s one of the big things that pissed me off.” 

Women in the focus group said that while they supported enforcing immigration laws and securing the border, they thought the government had gone too far. 

“I’m not against the deportation, I’m against inhumane treatment in that process,” said Kristen, the 39-year-old in Ohio. 

Brandy, a 43-year-old woman in North Carolina, said she was particularly troubled by federal immigration officials killing two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in Minnesota. She said when she posted about Good’s killing on Facebook, she was attacked by her friends who are “extreme Trump lovers.” 

“He just makes people lose their human decency,” she said. 

And they didn’t view other members of the Trump administration much more favorably. They used words like “terrible,” “compromised,” “Trump’s twin,” and “corrupt” to describe Vice President JD Vance. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was called “a liar,” and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “uneducated.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth “should have stayed on TV,” Kristen said. 

But despite the group’s collective distaste for Trump and his inner circle, not all plan to vote for Democrats down the ballot in November. 

Denise in Ohio said she was leaning toward voting for Democrat Amy Acton in Ohio’s race for governor over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, whom she described as “up [Trump’s] rear end,” while Gayle in Florida said she planned to vote for the Republican, Rep. Byron Donalds, in her state’s gubernatorial race. 

Brandy said she didn’t like former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in North Carolina, but was voting for him because of GOP nominee Michael Whatley’s ties to a convicted sex offender who served in several leadership positions in the state Republican Party, something Democratic groups have spent millions highlighting in campaign ads. 

“I’m gonna go for the guy that doesn’t have a buddy that’s a sex offender,” she said. “Even though I don’t like him, he is the lesser of two evils.” 

Toufanian said Democrats have a big opportunity to focus on issues suburban women care about “and to really make some tangible improvements in their lives.” 

Food quality and safety is one of those issues. Nearly all the women cited it as a top concern, but only two had heard of the acronym MAHA, or Make America Healthy Again. 

“I think there's a real opportunity because it touches on so many of the other issues that are so important in this election cycle, particularly corruption and affordability,” Toufanian said.

Most women in the focus group said they’re taking a wait-and-see approach to the 2028 presidential race. Two, Chrissy and Kristen, said they were open to voting for a Democrat but wouldn’t want to vote for Vance or former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee. 

Chrissy said she’d primarily evaluate Republican candidates on whether they would further the “cruelty” and “highly polarized” atmosphere cultivated by Trump. 

“I don't want the country to be identified like that anymore, at all. I don't even want to be a member. … I don't want to be a citizen of this country,” she said. “I'm embarrassed on a world stage.”

news.title: Jewish Opposition to Abdul El-Sayed May Not Matter in Michigan Race
news.text: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed told ABC News this week that he does not consider Israel an ally of the United States, his strongest statement yet on an issue that has drawn criticism and could affect his support among Jewish voters. “An ally that takes your money to push you into wars you shouldn’t be fighting is not an ally. It’s like, I mean, do you have kids?” El-Sayed replied when asked by ABC News anchor Linsey Davis whether he viewed Israel as an American ally. The remarks came a week after El-Sayed told MS NOW that the Israeli government had used the United States and done terrible things with American money. In an earlier debate, he declined to say whether Israel or Iran posed a greater threat to the United States. El-Sayed's views on Israel have drawn scrutiny since before he won the Democratic nomination in August, defeating U.S. Representative Haley Stevens in a race where AIPAC and its affiliated groups spent nearly $30 million trying to stop him. His description of Israel's war in Gaza as a "genocide" and his association with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker have also given Republican nominee Mike Rogers material for attacks, including accusations related to antisemitism. The question now is whether El-Sayed's increasingly blunt comments on Israel will cost him support among Jewish voters in a close race where every vote could matter. The ABC interview drew swift criticism online. Joe Walsh, former Republican congressman from Illinois who later became a Democrat, wrote that anyone who does not consider Israel a U.S. ally does not "belong in the U.S. Senate." Activist and writer Amy Siskind suggested this week that El-Sayed's campaign may be betting it can win without the support of most Jewish voters. Michigan's electoral demographics suggest that strategy could work. The state has roughly twice as many registered Muslim voters as Jewish voters. Many Muslim voters backed Green Party candidate Jill Stein or President Donald Trump in 2024, while others stayed home. If El-Sayed can win more of those voters back, their support could offset losses among Jewish Democrats. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed and Rogers campaigns for comment Tuesday. Michigan Muslim vs. Jewish Voters: How the Numbers Compare The Muslim voter advocacy group Emgage estimates there are more than 200,000 registered Muslim voters in Michigan. By comparison, Michigan is home to roughly 105,000 Jewish adults, about 1.4 percent of the state's electorate, according to the American Jewish Population Project at Brandeis University. Republican-aligned estimates run higher, up to 130,000. "It is important to remember that no state has a higher percentage of Arab-American residents in the U.S. than Michigan. The Jewish population is less than half that of the Arab-American population there," Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at the centrist Democratic think tank Third Way, told Newsweek. Arab American and Muslim are overlapping but distinct groups. Many of Michigan's Arab American residents are Chaldean and other Christians, while the state's Muslim community also includes South Asian and Black Muslims. Turnout narrows the gap, Kessler warns. Jewish voters participate at high rates. Muslim turnout has historically lagged. In the 2018 midterms, 50 percent of registered Muslim voters in Michigan cast ballots, according to Emgage. In 2024, a Council on American-Islamic Relations exit poll of Michigan Muslim voters found Stein received 59 percent support, Trump 22 percent and then-Vice President Kamala Harris 14 percent. Trump won more than 42 percent of the vote in Dearborn, where more than 55 percent of residents are of Middle Eastern descent, up from 30 percent four years earlier. Many others sat out. Early voting turnout was 25 percent in Dearborn and 24 percent in Hamtramck, against 44 percent statewide. Those voters already delivered for El-Sayed once. In the August primary, he got 16,265 more votes than Michigan Representative Haley Stevens across Dearborn and Dearborn Heights alone, more than his statewide margin over her of a little over 14,000 votes, in unofficial results. At a televised town hall on Monday, Rogers said he expects to win a sizable share of the state's roughly 70,000 Jewish Democrats. Winning half, he estimated, would add about 35,000 votes to his total. He lost his 2024 Senate race to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by 19,006 votes. Votes that switch sides count double. A Jewish Democrat who moves to Rogers shifts the margin by two, since El-Sayed loses one and Rogers picks one up. A Muslim voter coming back from a Stein ballot, or off the couch, adds one. Someone who voted Trump in 2024 and picks El-Sayed now adds two. Democratic Voters' Sympathy for Israel Hits Record Low Few Democrats in the Senate talk about Israel the way El-Sayed does. Gallup's numbers suggest the party's voters sit closer to him than to them. In Gallup's February survey, 65 percent of Democrats said their sympathies lie more with the Palestinians, while 17 percent said they sympathize more with the Israelis. In 2014, Democrats' sympathy for the Israelis peaked at 58 percent. For the first time since Gallup began asking the question a quarter-century ago, more Americans overall sided with the Palestinians, 41 percent to 36 percent. Many Democratic insiders also believe the issue cost the party the White House. Officials working on the Democratic National Committee's internal review of the 2024 election concluded that Harris lost support because of the Biden administration's approach to the war in Gaza, Axios reported. The IMEU Policy Project, a pro-Palestinian advocacy group, said DNC officials told its members that their own data found the policy was a "net negative." A YouGov poll commissioned by IMEU found that 29 percent of 2020 Biden voters who did not back Harris in 2024 named ending Israel's violence in Gaza as their top issue, ahead of the economy at 24 percent. In the six battleground states that flipped to Trump, the economy ranked first at 33 percent, with Gaza second at 20 percent. In Michigan, more than 100,000 Democrats voted "uncommitted" in the 2024 presidential primary, most heavily in Wayne County, home to Dearborn's Arab American community. Harris herself said last week that the Biden administration should have responded sooner to the Israeli government's conduct in Gaza. Temple Israel Attack, AIPAC Spending Fuel Antisemitism Concerns in Michigan On March 12, a man drove a fireworks-laden truck into Temple Israel, a Reform synagogue in West Bloomfield Township. The FBI later assessed it as a Hezbollah-inspired act of terrorism targeting the Jewish community. The attacker was the only person killed, and fear among Michigan Jews has not eased since. El-Sayed's first response drew backlash. He said there was never a justification for attacking innocent people, then added that violence is a cycle and that hurt people hurt people. Months later, at the state Democratic convention in August, he apologized to the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus. "I made a mistake," he told the group. His ties to left-wing streamer Hasan Piker have also drawn criticism. Pressed on the issue, El-Sayed told reporters, "this is not a campaign that is about a single streamer in California." The primary was shaped by record pro-Israel spending, the largest investment AIPAC has ever made in a single race. El-Sayed made the spending a centerpiece of his campaign. Stevens has since endorsed him, describing herself as a Democratic Zionist who wants to "be a part of stopping MAGA." Michigan's Jewish community is split. Roughly 500 people identifying as Jewish Democrats or independents signed an open letter calling Rogers a friend to the Jewish community. A separate letter released September 17 drew more than 620 Jewish voters who said they intend to vote for El-Sayed. The Jewish Democratic Council of America has not endorsed him, though its CEO, Halie Soifer, wrote that a vote for any Republican is a vote for Trump. No public poll has measured how Michigan's Jewish voters plan to vote in the race. Does Religion Decide Elections? El-Sayed Leans Into Muslim Faith El-Sayed has leaned into his own Islamic faith as Republican attacks on his religion have escalated. On Monday, his campaign released a 30-second ad that opens with four words: "My name is Abdul." Last week, Trump referred to El-Sayed as "Mohammed" and falsely called him a "jihadist." Rogers has pointed in debate to El-Sayed's mother's past work for the Islamic American Relief Agency, which the Treasury Department designated in 2004 as supporting terrorism. Yet neither the Jewish nor the Muslim community votes as a bloc. Some Jewish Democrats remain committed to El-Sayed, and some Muslim and Arab voters, many of them socially conservative, have backed Republicans before. Ask most Michigan voters what matters and they talk about prices. A Bridge Michigan survey found the economy is the biggest issue for Detroit-area voters, with others citing housing, affordability and health care, and El-Sayed has spent much of the campaign tying Rogers to Trump on costs and tariffs. Focus groups conducted by MS NOW found both Jewish voters in Oakland County and Muslim voters in Dearborn describing fears for their physical safety in similar terms. One Jewish participant who refuses to vote for El-Sayed said she also rejects Rogers because of advertising she described as racially charged. While religion may not be the main obstacle, winning over Black voters could be a bigger challenge for El-Sayed. Black voters make up roughly 11 to 12 percent of Michigan's electorate, compared with 1.5 to 2 percent who are Jewish. In a Washington Post poll, 83 percent of Black voters said they wanted Democrats to control the Senate, but only 67 percent said they would vote for El-Sayed. Latest Michigan Senate Polls: El-Sayed vs. Rogers El-Sayed has led in all five October polls included in the RCP average, and Rogers has not led any individual poll since early September. Pollsters warn the race could still shift. Mitchell Research & Communications said, "The race could tighten, perhaps dramatically," citing past Michigan Senate races where Republicans gained late. The RealClearPolitics polling average gives El-Sayed a 2.6-point lead over Rogers, based on polls completed between September 27 and October 14. That is down from a 3.4-point lead in the previous stretch. Republicans have not won a Senate race in Michigan since 1994. If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim U.S. senator.
