news.text:
ANALYSIS — Another week and we have another batch of race rating changes by Inside Elections, all in favor of Democrats. With just two weeks to go before the general election, Republicans are running out of time to change the trajectory of the midterms. President Donald Trump’s job approval rating is mired in the high 30s, and the GOP is at risk of losing its majorities on Capitol Hill. 

The Senate battleground

The Senate battleground continues to shift and evolve in Democrats’ favor. New Hampshire, where Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen is retiring, shifts from Toss-up to Tilt Democratic. That means Democrats don’t have any defensive seats in races rated a Toss-up or worse, making it easier for them to gain the four seats necessary for a majority. 

Ratings also shifted in four Republican states that were all rated Solid Republican at the beginning of the cycle. Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years and yet the race between GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton is very competitive. That race moves from Likely Republican to Tilt Republican, one step away from Toss-up. 

Two appointed senators, Darline Graham of South Carolina and Ashley Moody of Florida, can’t take their races for granted. The Palmetto State shifts from Likely Republican to Lean Republican, while the Sunshine State moves from Solid Republican to Likely Republican. 

Even though Democrats always seem to fall short in Texas, their nominee, state Rep. James Talarico, has maintained a very narrow advantage over Republican Ken Paxton, leading by a point or two for five months. Paxton, the state attorney general, could still win, but Talarico’s lead has been durable and undeniable. That race shifts from Tilt Republican to Toss-up, the same rating as the contests in Alaska, Maine and Ohio. 

Inside Elections’ current Senate projection is a Democratic gain of three to five seats, a range that spans the four needed for a majority. 

The House landscape

Democratic prospects are better in the House, where the party needs a net gain of just three seats for the majority, with a much larger pool of opportunities compared with the Senate.

Races for the more evenly divided districts at the center of the House battlefield have been stubbornly close despite Trump’s poor job approval rating. But Democrats’ list of potential takeovers has grown as GOP voters wrestle with disappointment over the lack of a promised economic rebound and contemplate which party to vote for or whether to vote at all.

As I wrote recently, Republicans are having particular difficulty defending open seats. Without incumbents with established identities who might be able to withstand a political storm, the party is struggling to win several districts deep in GOP territory. 

Nearly half of Inside Elections’ recent House rating changes — 10 out of 22 races — involved GOP-held open seats, all in favor of Democrats. 

It’s not a surprise Republicans are struggling to hold Nebraska’s open 2nd District, where Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump in 2024. But the most of the other nine changes are in districts that backed Trump by anywhere from 10 points to more than 20 points. 

The race ratings for Arizona’s 1st, Iowa’s 2nd, Kentucky’s 6th, Montana’s 1st, Nevada’s 2nd, New York’s 21st, North Carolina’s 11th, South Carolina’s 1st and even Wyoming’s at-large district all shifted toward Democrats. 

The open seat in Wyoming, held by Senate hopeful Harriet M. Hageman, is among four Republican new additions to the House battleground. It joins Arkansas’ 2nd District (represented by French Hill), Indiana’s 5th (Victoria Spartz) and Nebraska’s 1st (Mike Flood) in moving from Solid Republican to Likely Republican. Meanwhile, two Democratic seats shifted in the other direction, with New Jersey’s 9th District (Nellie Pou) and New York’s 19th (Josh Riley) going from Likely Democratic to Solid Democratic. 

Two more GOP incumbents are now underdogs as the races for Pennsylvania’s 7th District (Ryan Mackenzie) and 8th (Rob Bresnahan Jr.) shift from Toss-up to Tilt Democratic. And three Democratic incumbents who were targeted by Republicans for defeat through redistricting are still hanging on. Rating prospects improved for Shomari Figures (Alabama’s 2nd), Don Davis (North Carolina’s 1st) and Marcy Kaptur (Ohio’s 9th). 

Inside Elections currently projects a Democratic gain of 10 to 20 House seats, well above what the party needs for the majority. It’s possible Republicans will boost their turnout enough to avert disaster and win a few dozen races by uncomfortably close margins. But it’s also possible such a turnout won’t materialize and Republicans will end up losing dozens of races by narrow margins in a historic blowout. 

Elections for governor

Two states have joined the gubernatorial battleground, with the reelection efforts of Govs. Jim Pillen of Nebraska and Phil Scott of Vermont now looking less of a sure thing. Those races move from Solid Republican to Likely Republican. 

In Texas, GOP Gov. Greg Abbott remains favored to win a record fourth term, but Democratic nominee Gina Hinojosa has proved to be his toughest challenger yet. The race moves from Likely Republican to Lean Republican.

news.title: Democrats fear slippage with Black voters makes Michigan Senate race feel ‘far closer than it should’
news.text: Abdul El-Sayed often talks about building a new and broad coalition of Michigan voters. A looming question in the state’s pivotal Senate race is whether he can keep the old one intact — particularly with the Black voters who are pivotal to any Democratic victory.The Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has spent months working to make inroads with traditional Democratic constituencies that did not support El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, in his bitter primary battle against Rep. Haley Stevens.POLITICAL ANALYSIS | Battle for the control of CongressAnd even though more than $280 million has been spent on television advertisements in Michigan since the 2026 midterm election cycle began, with billboards and campaign yard signs dotting the landscape alongside the fall colors, some political leaders wonder whether there is sufficient enthusiasm among Black voters for El-Sayed at this late stage.“It only takes this much of Detroit to defect. It only takes this much of Flint to defect,” said the Rev. Charles Williams II, pastor of the Historic King Solomon Baptist Church in Detroit, holding his fingers about an inch apart to drive home his point. “If even a sliver of people don’t turn out, you run into a huge challenge in trying to get your candidate over that line.”Holding the Democratic coalitionMichigan is crucial to Democrats’ hopes of the net four-seat gain the party needs on November 3 to win control of the Senate. If the party fails to retain the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, its path to a majority would grow much more difficult — and would run almost exclusively through much redder states than this upper Midwestern perpetual political battleground.El-Sayed defeated Stevens in the August primary by just 1 percentage point — a narrow victory fueled by his strong support among Arab American and Muslim communities, young voters and progressives in college towns.But Stevens had clear strengths, too: Black voters in and around Detroit largely aligned behind her, as did Jewish voters who have long expressed deep concerns with El-Sayed, who is Muslim and a strident critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Poll: El Sayed holds slight edge in Michigan Senate race, but struggles with older swing votersRogers has made reaching those constituencies a central focus of his campaign in the race’s closing weeks, as he looks to assemble a coalition of voters more favorable to Republicans than in 2018, the last midterm election with President Donald Trump in office. That year, Democrats won four statewide races in Michigan, all by a range of about 7 to 9 percentage points.At a Detroit Economic Club forum on Tuesday, Rogers bragged that he has “built coalitions that really are very untraditional for a Republican candidate.”He pointed to plans to incentivize new home construction in Detroit, connect those construction efforts to high school apprenticeships, and eliminate “food deserts” in the city. He also said many Democrats have told him they fear the rising influence of democratic socialists within the party.“We’ve spent a lot of time here in Detroit, Flint, Pontiac,” he said, listing cities with large Black populations. “I think if we’re going to get our state right, we have to have everybody included in its forward progress.”In a bid to ease lingering Democratic doubts about El-Sayed, former President Barack Obama is set to visit Michigan, where he’ll attend a Saturday rally in Detroit with El-Sayed and the party’s nominee for governor, Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson.Other prominent Black Democrats have visited Michigan in recent weeks, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, who held a roundtable focused on Black maternal healthcare with El-Sayed. Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia is also set to campaign with El-Sayed, as are several members of the Congressional Black Caucus.“As much as he thinks he’s making inroads, folks are smart,” El-Sayed told CNN. “Mike Rogers is simply a rubber stamp on what Donald Trump wants. They understand exactly who Mike Rogers is.”While conversations with Black leaders and voters across Detroit show widespread support for El-Sayed, quiet concerns emerged about whether questions pertaining to the nominee’s background could dampen support. Historic tensions between Arab American and Black communities also were raised as points of anxiety.“In a close race, even a sliver of doubt about Abdul could lead to defeat,” one prominent Black leader told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss concerns frankly. “And this race feels far closer than it should.”El-Sayed mocks Rogers’ Black outreachEven as prominent Black Democratic leaders in Michigan express concern about the Senate race, El-Sayed — who spent recent days campaigning in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, a sparsely populated region where he hopes his populist pitch will chip away at the GOP’s traditionally strong margins — is downplaying and even mocking Rogers’ efforts to win over Black voters.At a campaign stop in Flint, a majority-Black city, a few hundred supporters turned out for an El-Sayed rally on Sunday afternoon. Only about a dozen members of the audience who packed into a large hotel conference room were Black, which was striking for a Democratic campaign event two weeks before the election.As he spoke to reporters afterward, El-Sayed said he saw no reason for concern.“Look, one of the hardest things about this economy is that too often folks are having to work multiple jobs and having to work on weekends,” he told CNN. “We know because of exactly the policies architected by folks like Donald Trump, that falls hardest on Black folks.”He was joined at the rally by Democratic Rep. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, one of several Black members of Congress who have traveled to campaign alongside him.“We feel really strong about the relationship we’ve built and will continue to build,” El-Sayed said of his outreach to Black voters.When asked about the Rogers campaign opening a storefront office on Livernois Avenue in Detroit as part of its effort to win over Black voters, El-Sayed answered with a laugh.“I saw he opened a cute little office in Detroit where he brought all his friends from the suburbs to come clap him in. It was nice, yeah,” El-Sayed said. “He’s got no actual message for anyone who is struggling to make ends meet.”RELATED STORY | Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tours for Michigan progressive Abdul El-Sayed in close Senate raceMarcia Turner, who attended the Flint rally, said she was optimistic about El-Sayed, who she called “the right person at the right time.” But even her kind words underscored a history of some tension between the Black and Arab communities of Michigan.“I love that he’s running,” Turner said. “I think people are looking past his religion and seeing him as a man who wants what we want for our children and grandchildren.”Rogers steps ‘out of his space’Naura Evans, a teacher and mother of two from Sterling Heights, is a proud Black Republican. She appears in a television commercial, saying: “I voted for Barack Obama, but this year, I’m voting for Mike Rogers.”She said she grew up in a Democratic family but has become more conservative since her 2008 vote for Obama. She said she thinks schools and neighborhoods haven’t improved under Democratic rule and believes in Rogers’ plans for both.She said she feels that Democrats have taken Black voters for granted over the years, so she spends time going door-to-door in Warren, Troy and Sterling Heights, trying to persuade voters to join her in supporting Rogers.“It’s very important that we elect the right people,” Evans said. “As Blacks in our community, we show that our vote matters. We’re not just giving the vote away.”She said the Rogers campaign should get credit for opening an office in Detroit.“I’ve seen Mike Rogers definitely step out of his space and go into the Black community,” Evans said. “I think it’s practical and I think it’s also symbolic that he cares about Detroit. He could have opened an office anywhere and he chose Detroit.”She dismissed one of the biggest pieces of criticism she hears from Democrats about Rogers — that he would be a rubber stamp for Trump.“This is not a presidential election, it’s a senator’s election, and ultimately Mike Rogers will be the one making his own decisions,” Evans said. “I’m sure that his decisions will not be influenced by someone else.”‘His culture is different’Quentin Murray listened to the full slate of Democratic candidates speaking at a carpenters’ union hall on Sunday in Detroit. He said he was just beginning to learn more about El-Sayed’s candidacy but liked what he heard.“I like what he’s bringing to the table — something new, something different,” said Murray, a carpenter. “His culture is different, but when you see somebody like that, it’s good to know that we have the same interests and values.”Yet even in his praise, Murray casually brought up El-Sayed’s culture, which has been at the center of the campaign in bitter attack ads about his upbringing and beliefs.El-Sayed, a doctor and former public health official whose parents immigrated to the US from Egypt, was born and raised in Michigan.At nearly every campaign stop, he briefly explains his family history and pushes back at some of the racially charged conversations about his name, which has been regularly belittled by Trump, who has taken to calling him “Mohammed Abdul El-Sayed.”Rogers has attempted to connect El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood — which El-Sayed has denounced — and cast him as sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terror. The GOP has pointed to old tweets from his sister describing El-Sayed’s birth mother’s activism with the Muslim Brotherhood while she was in college in the early 1970s. In a recent debate, Rogers also pointed out that El-Sayed’s mother worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency, a nonprofit that the Treasury Department in 2004 designated as an organization supporting terrorism. El-Sayed was primarily raised by his father and stepmother in Michigan.“My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas. My name and my faith are not the reason you cannot afford your groceries,” El-Sayed told supporters in Flint. “My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t see a doctor. I mean chances are if you’re seeing a doctor, they might actually have my name and my faith.”A progressive’s bid to win over moderatesCharity Dean, who owns a Detroit coffee shop and is president of the Michigan Black Business Alliance, said she has been pleasantly surprised by the enthusiasm for El-Sayed in her city.“Detroit is more conservative than folks would think — a lot more moderate,” Dean said. “I think his campaign has done a phenomenal job of really busting out of the box and saying, ‘Are you happy with how things are now? Are you happy with forever wars?’”Since finishing a distant second in Detroit in the August primary, Dean said, El-Sayed has listened to voters — supportive and skeptical ones alike — and has worked to build a campaign to win them over.“One of the things that’s gained him a lot of ground is his ability to respond to criticism and questions,” Dean said.While Dean said she has seen many signs that Rogers is trying to expand his outreach to Black voters, including television ads and opening an office in Detroit, she questioned whether the Republican nominee’s policies followed suit with the actions of his campaign.“Everything should be taken seriously. This is not a year where we take anything for granted,” Dean said, noting that she is carefully watching what the Rogers campaign is doing. “He seriously wants to win their vote, but he doesn’t want to make life better for Black people. That’s what really matters.”The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros. Discovery Company. All rights reserved.
news.summary: Michigan's Senate race could decide control of the chamber — and it may come down to Black voters in Detroit and Flint. Where do you think the race stands?

news.title: Young Men Are Abandoning the ‘Pod Bros’ Who Got Trump Elected
news.text:
Podcasters who peddled and laundered Donald Trump to victory in 2024 are hemorrhaging their one-time biggest fans: Young men. 

Trump took to podcasts like The Joe Rogan Experience and This Past Weekend with Theo Von to boost his numbers among economically disaffected young white voters, while Kamala Harris failed to gain ground with them. But amid his tumultuous term, Trump has had a contagious effect on most of the figures who propelled him back to the top. 

Puck has revealed that individuals in the right-wing media sphere, including Tucker Carlson, Andrew Tate, and Joe Rogan, have all experienced double-digit drops in approval ratings since publicly backing Trump in 2024.

War with Iran marked a turning point for the young men who helped to carry Trump to victory, devastating the economy and breaking key policy promises that distinguished it from the Harris campaign, a polling expert told Puck. 

After feeling the blow of Trump’s newfound unpopularity, nearly all of the so-called Pod Bros have attempted to make like the voters and distance themselves from Trump. 

Carlson, who interviewed and endorsed Trump on the campaign trail after Fox News fired him in 2023, has seen his favorability among young men drop 12 points in the last year. Carlson began walking back his role in getting Trump elected immediately after Trump launched a war with Iran. 

“I do think it’s like a moment to wrestle with our own consciences,” Carlson said. “We’ll be tormented by it for a long time. I will be. And I want to say I’m sorry for misleading people.” 

Rogan, who has tried to bill himself as an independent “free-thinker” despite latching hard onto Trump in 2024, has also seemingly wised up. 

“What Trump stood for, some of it turned out to not be real,” Rogan said during a podcast with actor Michael Douglas this month. “Like one of them was ‘No wars’... That wasn’t real.”

Rogan rejects the idea that Democrats were any better, but has had little positive to say about the current White House. Young men, who make up a majority of Rogan’s audience, approve of the Podcaster 11 points less than when Trump was elected. 

Young men who hoped to see less “wokeness” and scold culture in 2024 are now more likely to favor figures like Sen. Bernie Sanders, Barack Obama, and Zohran Mamdani, according to Puck’s reporting. 

During an April episode of his podcast, Theo Von illustrated what young men may be feeling ahead of the midterm elections. 

“Besides the war, the industrial war complex, what American... what guy who’s trying to take care of his family or a single mother who’s a nurse who’s going to work and has to get home and get to her kid’s ballgame... What farmer is this helping? What regular person is this helping? I just don’t know. I don’t understand.”

news.title: Fans Crash Out as TV Star Says She ‘Prefers Trump’
news.text:
Poker Face star Natasha Lyonne has fans confused after she posted a series of social media messages suggesting her views on Donald Trump have softened. 

Lyonne, just months after the media firestorm over her removal from a Delta Air Lines flight in April, posted a string of emojis that appeared to support Trump’s praise of Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Tuesday. 

“A BIG THANK YOU to our legendary friend, @ElonMusk, for his incredible generosity in giving SpaceX Stock to millions of American children through TRUMP ACCOUNTS!” Trump wrote, a year and a half after Musk posted on X that he was “in the Epstein files.” The president added, “This is exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS… Thank you Elon!” 

Lyonne reposted the comments, with the emoji message, “🚀🫡☀️😎.” 

Baffled fans flooded the post to reply. “You’re too cool to believe this stupid s--t,” one wrote. 

“Damn, it sucks to see someone you like publicly reveal themselves to be a complete self-oblivious idiot,” wrote another. “Welp, you’ve lost a fan.” 

One hopeful wrote, “Please tell me this means you want to launch them into the sun and watch?” while another wrote simply, “Girl, no.”

Added yet another, “She’s not MAGA. This has to be sarcasm. Pls clarify, Queen.”

The Daily Beast has reached out to a representative for Lyonne for comment. 

Her previous post was a recirculation of a clip showing Vice President JD Vance using a vile immigrant smear to dismiss a protester at a rally. She wrote, “Sketchy mofo—prefer Trump—this s--t is even scarier—don’t really know how we arrived at this aesthetic as baseline normal, but c’est la dominoes, etc. Octavia Butler was a soothsayer. Grimey times.” 

When a commenter asked her to clarify what she meant by “Prefer Trump,” Lyonne wrote, “To insert Manchurian Candidate here?”

In January 2026, Lyonne shared on social media that she had relapsed after nearly a decade of sobriety. The actress has been open about her battle with heroin addiction, as well as cocaine and alcohol use, in the early-to-mid 2000s. 

In April 2026, Lyonne was escorted off a Delta flight from Los Angeles to New York amid claims that she appeared disoriented and did not respond to flight attendants who had repeatedly asked her to close her laptop and fasten her seatbelt. She later apologized, saying she had taken a sleeping pill.

Her latest comments on the Trump administration appear at odds with her previous statements. 

In February 2025, she shared her thoughts on “orange” Trump with The Hollywood Reporter. “It’s very weird to have a showbiz guy in charge; it’s surreal. I mean, because, well, I’m actually pretty horrified by how strategic and effective this whole thing has been.”

She added, “I think there’s a real disconnect and all of the noise around the individuals that are going to be really taking the hits on an individual, human basis in the trans community, gay community, black community, women. I hate violence so much, and I just think that’s the part of it.”

In May, she told Glamour she wasn’t “a fan” of Trump’s, and endorsed Kamala Harris a few months later.

Obsessed with pop culture and entertainment? Follow us on Substack and YouTube for even more coverage.
news.summary:
REUTERS/Mario AnzuoniPoker Face star Natasha Lyonne has fans confused after she posted a series of social media messages suggesting her views on Donald Trump have softened. 

Lyonne, just months after the media firestorm over her removal from a Delta Air Lines flight in April, posted a string of emojis that appeared to support Trump’s praise of Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Tuesday. 

“A BIG THANK YOU to our legendary friend, @ElonMusk, for his incredible generosity in giving SpaceX Stock to millions of American children through TRUMP ACCOUNTS!” Trump wrote, a year and a half after Musk posted on X that he was “in the Epstein files.” The president added, “This is exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS… Thank you Elon!” 

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: Steven Bartlett started ‘The Diary of a CEO’ with a $100 microphone. Now he says it’s on track for $60 million in annual revenue
news.text:
The show has grown into a business Bartlett forecasts will generate about $60 million in revenue this year. But growing it has also meant turning down money—including a deal that would have required more advertising and taking the show off YouTube. He described the proposed arrangement as a trade: Accept a large payment, put 12 advertisements in the podcast, and have little say over those ads.

“One of the central reasons why I turned down such an offer is because that is four times more ads than I have to put in now,” Bartlett told Fortune’s Ellie Austin on Fortune Daily.

Working with what he calls “fragmentation vultures”—companies seeking exclusive podcast distribution deals—can mean sacrificing revenue or control over the relationship with an audience, Bartlett argued. Instead, he sees the relationship with his audience as worth protecting, even when a lucrative offer like that comes along. The business he aims to preserve already makes money beyond advertising through products, subscriptions, and events.

Beyond the podcast ad

Bartlett, who dropped out of college to pursue entrepreneurship, launched The Diary of a CEO in 2017 by turning his own diary entries into podcast episodes. He later began interviewing other people about their own diaries, finding it more intellectually stimulating to learn about their own lives than to read about his own.

Those conversations explored his guests’ motivations, insecurities, and ambitions, eventually broadening the show’s scope to subjects ranging from neuroscience and psychology to performance and sports. 

And with it, the business has expanded too. When asked where the show’s projected $60 million comes from, Bartlett pointed to brand partnerships, products his business owns and manufactures, subscriptions, memberships, and events. On top of that, he runs an investment fund. 

“It’s a wide range of things and again, this goes to the point of diversification,” he said.

Steven.com, Bartlett’s holding company, houses the podcast and his other creator businesses. It also includes other creators, helping them build media brands and develop products and ventures. Bartlett forecasts about $90 million in revenue for his broader media company this year, including the projected $60 million from The Diary of a CEO. 

He also put next year’s holding-company forecast at about $160 million. But he’s not the only person to see nine-figure valuations as a result of the podcasting business: Call Her Daddy podcast host Alex Cooper’s holding company Unwell raised investment at a $500 million valuation in August.

Bartlett sees that evolution as part of a wider shift of how creators work with brands. Early in his career, he said companies treated influencers like billboards: Pay them, and they would post something. Then came the creative-director titles, equity arrangements, and opportunities to cofound businesses. That is most evident with Sydney Sweeney, who became an equity partner and creative director at sports prediction market Novig, shaping its advertising rather than just simply appearing in it.

He believes the next stage involves creator businesses making acquisitions and operating more like large holding companies. 

“You’re no longer an influencer, you’re no longer an equity partner, a creative director,” he said. “You are an owner or cofounder.”

The business of audience trust

Distribution has become a point of negotiation across podcasting, perhaps most famously in 2024, when Spotify ended Rogan’s exclusivity and allowed his show to stream on rival platforms. Bartlett prefers fewer partnerships, and only with businesses that matter to him personally. About 70% of his podcast partners, he said, are companies whose founders he approached himself. 

Choosing sponsors is only one part of maintaining audience trust—what guests say on the podcast matters too. On Fortune Daily, he was questioned about a 2024 BBC investigation into health claims made on his show. He said his team had contracted a full-time medical PhD to review health episodes, adding context on screen and removing material that could not adequately be contextualized. Now, an independent review team fact-checks every episode—not just those focused on health—before it is published. 

When asked whether an unsupported scientific statement would be removed from the audio, he said the decision depends on its framing: A definitive claim would be treated differently from a guest discussing a hypothesis based on early research.

But despite his growing influence, Bartlett doesn’t consider himself a journalist. He described his interviews as an exercise in pursuing his own curiosity, whether he’s sitting across from Kamala Harris or JD Vance. Viewers will always have questions they wish he had asked, he said, but he believes his approach needs to remain anchored in that curiosity.

“If you’re not anchored to, like, your own curiosity, you’re going to be a plastic bag in the wind,” he said.

As the business continues to grow, Bartlett’s advice to other creators is to think beyond the next deal—while acknowledging that his own success gives him more freedom to choose. 

“If you want to build a durable business in this creator economy, you have to prioritize sovereignty,” he said. “You’re renting your audience at the moment.”
news.summary: The podcast host says he rejected a deal that would have meant more ads and leaving YouTube. Now his business extends beyond sponsorships.
news.author: Tatiana Sataua

news.title: Democrats Pouring Money Into Campaign For Mississippi Senate Seat Party Hasn’t Held Since 1980s
news.text:
Senate Democrats’ top campaign spending arm planned to spend $1.2 million in deep red Mississippi Tuesday while their candidate performed well in the polls. 

The Senate Majority PAC intends to air the new television advertisement in support of Democratic Mississippi Senate nominee Scott Colom ahead of his race against Republican Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, The Associated Press first reported. The ad is set to start Wednesday and air through Election Day. 

“Senate Majority PAC has been watching this race closely, and it is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” the PAC’s spokesperson Lauren French said. 

Senate Majority PAC (D) announces its first spending in Mississippi It’ll start a $1.2 million TV ad campaign there Wednesday through Election Day, per an SMP spox #MSSEN— Patrick Svitek (@PatrickSvitek) October 20, 2026

A Wedgwood Polls survey found Colom trailing Hyde-Smith 52% to 48%, while other polls found Hyde-Smith leading by single digits. Mississippi last elected a Democratic U.S. senator in November 1982 and both its Senate seats have been controlled by Republicans since 1989. (RELATED: Ranchers Say Trump’s Beef Imports Have GOP Senator Mike Rounds ‘Treading Water’ In South Dakota)

President Donald Trump won 60.9% of the vote in Mississippi during the 2024 presidential election. 

Only $8 million has been spent in the Senate race, with Colom outspending Hyde-Smith nearly $4.6 million to $3.2 million, The Associated Press reported. 

Colom campaigned with Democratic Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and is scheduled to rally with former Vice President Kamala Harris on Thursday. 

The Democratic candidate centered his campaign around affordability, which is the top issue for voters in the election cycle, according to his campaign website. He is also district attorney for Mississippi’s 16th Judicial District, giving him name recognition. 

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in May that Louisiana’s racially gerrymandered map was unconstitutional, prompting the Mississippi state Legislature considered redistricting to redraw black majority districts. The Mississippi state Legislature initially planned to redraw Mississippi’s lone majority-black district, although Republican Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves canceled a planned special legislative session on redistricting in May after receiving backlash from constituents. 

Charles Taylor, executive director of the Mississippi state conference of the NAACP, said rising costs motivated Democratic voters across the state, according to The Washington Post. He highlighted how the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision mobilized black voters. 

Thousands of protesters rallied in Jackson to protest the redistricting efforts and mobilized people to vote in November, according to Mississippi Today, a local outlet. Black voters make up roughly 35% of Mississippi’s voting population, according to The Washington Post. 

The Senate Majority PAC launched a $5 million television ad campaign in Kansas, a state that has not had a Democratic senator since 1939. It also spent tens of millions in Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska. 

Democrats pulled spending from Georgia and North Carolina while Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Democratic North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper held comfortable leads. 

Republican PACs spent over $326 million to support Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton while he fell behind Democratic Texas Senate nominee James Talarico. It spent $14 million to support Republican Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall and $5 million for Republican South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham.
news.summary: ‘Colom is running a competitive race’
news.author: Nicole Silverio

news.title: Is Kamala Harris Running for President in 2028? Everything to Know About The Ex-Veep's Political Career Plans
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris has made clear that she is considering another presidential campaign, but she has not committed to running in 2028.

Harris addressed the possibility most directly in April 2026 during a conversation with Rev. Al Sharpton at the National Action Network convention in New York. 

Asked whether she would launch another White House bid, she replied, “Listen, I might, I might. I’m thinking about it.”Harris Breaks Silence on 2028 RunHarris’ comments represented her strongest public indication yet that she could seek the presidency again after losing the 2024 election to Donald Trump.

She also pointed to her experience as vice president when explaining why another campaign remains under consideration. 

“I spent countless hours in the Oval Office, in the Situation Room. I know what the job is. And I know what it requires,” she said.

She continued, “I’ve been traveling the country the last year; I’ve spent a lot of time in the South and many other places. And the one thing I’m really clear about also is that the status quo is not working, and hasn’t been working for a lot of people for a long time.”Her Memoir and Political Tour Have Kept Her in the SpotlightHarris’ political activity has continued since her 2024 defeat. She released 107 Days, her memoir about the abbreviated presidential campaign, on Sept. 23, 2025. 

The book chronicles the 107-day campaign that began after then-President Joe Biden withdrew from the race.

During a BBC interview with Laura Kuenssberg in October 2025, Harris also said, “I am not done,” while acknowledging that she had not decided what she would do next. 

She said she could “possibly” become president in the future.

Harris subsequently announced that she would not run for California governor in 2026, leaving a potential 2028 presidential campaign as one possible path back into elected politics.Harris Continues to Criticize TrumpHarris has remained an outspoken critic of Trump since leaving office.

At the National Action Network convention, she condemned his handling of the conflict with Iran, calling it a “war of choice.” 

She also argued that Trump’s approach to longstanding U.S. alliances, including NATO, was damaging to American influence and national security.

Her political activity has continued into the 2026 midterm campaign. 

Harris is scheduled to campaign for Democratic candidates in several states from Oct. 21 through Oct. 30, including New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Mississippi, Nevada, and Georgia, along with a virtual event in Florida.A Crowded Democratic Field AwaitsHarris would face a potentially crowded Democratic primary if she ultimately decides to run.

The National Action Network convention also featured possible 2028 contenders including Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego. 

Several Democrats have avoided committing to a presidential campaign while focusing on the 2026 midterms. That leaves Harris with a clear opening to keep building her national profile without formally entering the 2028 race.
news.summary: Kamala Harris appeared at the National Action Network Convention in New York, saying that she is considering to run for president in 2028

news.title: How Jill Biden Concealed the President’s Rapid Deterioration
news.text:
But America in 2020 was in a darker, more polarized place than during the Obama years. Biden inherited an economically anxious country traumatized by COVID-19. Schools across the country were toggling between closures and online learning. Jill was one of the few messengers in the administration who resonated with mothers and teachers, who was a teacher herself., She quickly took up what she described as an unexpected “healing role.” Many states had shockingly low vaccination rates, and in the summer of 2021, Jill traveled to states like Mississippi and Tennessee telling communities their rates were “not enough.” Sometimes she got booed for the unwelcome message. “Well, you’re booing yourselves,” she told a crowd in Nashville, who then went silent.
Staff in her East Wing knew they weren’t getting a honeymoon period. The office would need to help transition the country back to normalcy at the same time as it launched its own projects and agenda. It was an ambitious goal. But Jill did not appoint superstars, she set up her office much like the Biden White House, filled with trusted friends and family retainer types, staffers whose careers had been built around the Bidens.
Looming over them all was Anthony Bernal, the fifty-something, square, dark-suited, veteran of Bidenland, and Jill Biden’s senior advisor. Bernal was Latino by background, a native of Tucson, Arizona, who had studied history at the University of Texas, and worked his way up in Democratic politics. He began working for the Bidens in 2008, and his forte was not policy or politicking but events. Even his critics acknowledged he had a gift for running polished, lively productions: campaign rallies, fundraisers, intricate foreign trips. While in Jill’s office he had the amorphous title of senior advisor, in the White House he was an assistant to the president, at the very top of the hierarchy. Bernal was blunt, domineering, and divisive.
He would be called, in the course of the next four years: part of the “cabal of the unhelpful,” the Biden “marriage counselor,” Jill’s “work husband,” “the loyalty police,” an office bully, and a top member of the Biden “Politburo,” the tight circle of aides who later allegedly concealed the president’s deterioration from the public and his cabinet.
Anthony Bernal adored Jill. Her political future was his. For Bernal, a second Biden term was a given, and he often floated ideas for Jill’s second East Wing. “He never stopped wanting to hold her purse,” said one insider. “I think he would crawl into the coffin with her.”
During the early weeks of Jill Biden’s tenure, her staff observed her relationship with Bernal, who appeared both the mastermind and enforcer of her approach. With time it would become clear that Jill’s choices—the events she attended, the strategy behind her travel schedule, the projects she took up, her interventions and her silences—were all fanatically devoted to propping up Joe.
At the outset, liberals especially hoped that Jill Biden would be Melania Trump’s opposite, an openly progressive, activist First Lady; these were oversize expectations for a woman who, up to that point, had kept a fairly traditional public persona as supportive political wife and mother, with a nonthreatening career as a teacher.
But over the course of four years, her First Ladyship unfolded as exceedingly narrow, even conservative. She never pursued a distinct project through which the public could get a sense of her—of her personality, what she cared about, and the texture of her beliefs and commitments. She stood steadfastly by her man and squeezed herself into such a narrow, Joe-centric persona that public opinion about the two of them essentially merged. In polls, both during and at the end of Joe’s presidency, a third of people viewed her unfavorably and a third had no opinion of her.
One by one, Biden’s staffers dialed into the emergency call. A disaster was barreling toward the Biden administration, and the purpose of the call was to discuss how to shield the First Lady. After two decades of war, the US military was withdrawing from Afghanistan, and Kabul was falling. In the span of just ten days in August, the Afghan government collapsed, the president fled in a helicopter, and a suicide bombing at Kabul airport killed 13 US soldiers and 170 civilians. The administration was bungling the withdrawal and struggled to evacuate American citizens and Afghan allies amid the chaos. Word spread across the city that the Taliban had kill lists of Afghan women activists, and hundreds of terrified women went into hiding. It was a dark moment for the Biden administration, and inside the East Wing, Afghanistan had become a third rail.
On the emergency call, staffers discussed halting events for Joining Forces, Jill’s joint initiative focused on supporting families of the Armed Forces that began under the Obama administration, and stopping all activities that might expose the First Lady to public anger or questioning about Afghanistan. “They had a huge fear of doing anything at bases, they were just petrified,” said the former staffer. “Even though this was when military communities needed support.” The catastrophic exit from Afghanistan was devastating to many veterans who had served there. Watching the Taliban regain power called into question the meaning of their sacrifice, and the government’s difficulty evacuating Afghan comrades who had fought with them felt like a betrayal.
Jill finally resumed visiting with military service members who had been involved in the withdrawal or their families. She traveled to Camp Lejeune, in North Carolina, where one of the young female soldiers killed in the Kabul airport attack had been based. But no one saw it because the East Wing, in a sharp departure from usual practice, had refused to allow press.
Since the 1990s, the East Wing had what could almost be called a compact with Afghan women. If there was any pocket of women’s activism in the world that the United States, particularly the Office of the First Lady owned and owed, it was Afghan women.
Hillary Clinton and Laura Bush mobilized their usual networks to mount independent missions to evacuate Afghan women. But while Hillary and Laura were hard at work, Jill Biden appeared to have gone missing. A calculation had been made in the East Wing that it would be damaging for her to address the fallout for Afghan women, even though Jill was uniquely placed to address the challenges facing them.
The Virginia community where the First Lady taught was a reception point and support hub for hundreds of Afghans evacuated after the fall of Kabul. The college was a longtime hub for Afghan women students; Jill had taught and worked with them herself. It was hard to understand why, as a First Lady who championed education and women, she had nothing to say. “Where are your outspoken voices on justice and education for women and girls of Afghanistan?” demanded an Afghan activist, addressing Jill, as well as Kamala Harris, the first female vice president
By the end of that turbulent summer, the East Wing also lost its chief of staff. Julissa Reynoso had the actual title, but it was Anthony Bernal who was calling the shots. At the end of July, only six months into the term, it was announced that she would be leaving, nominated by Biden as US ambassador to Spain.
Jill’s approach to being First Lady was to act as Joe’s lead messenger, and this suited Bernal, who had gained his knowledge of policy indirectly as a scheduler and advance man. Her activities never took him out of his comfort zone. Instead, Bernal excelled as the guardian of the Bidens’ privacy, and this made him indispensable and the sole staffer in the East Wing to hold real power. In the White House, said LaRosa, Bernal had unique latitude. “Bernal was her speechwriter, policy director, image maker, body person, personal assistant, press secretary, he was everything,” he said. “He was infinitely more powerful than the White House chief of staff.”
In early June 2024, Jill Biden flew across the Atlantic three times in the course of a week. She spent Monday, her seventy-third birthday, and the following two days at a courthouse in Wilmington, Delaware, at the federal trial of Hunter Biden, who was accused of lying about his drug use when buying a gun. On Thursday she flew to France to join the president for D-Day celebrations, and returned in less than twenty-four hours to be back at Hunter’s trial on Friday. The next day she flew back to France to join the president’s state visit. Joe was known to dislike it when she was absent and would grow ill-tempered when they were apart. Jill’s frenetic comings and goings that week attested to the long-running strains on her personally, dealing with the Bidens’ troubled family life while Joe did his job being president.
The trial in June gained a particular power through its timing. It fell during the exact moment when a movement was gaining steam to push the president out of the race, the very month when Joe needed to be sharp and ready for his debate with Donald Trump. Some aides would later say he deteriorated rapidly right around this time, during Hunter’s traumatic trial. It was the same month he didn’t recognize George Clooney at a fundraiser, alarmed bigwig donors by appearing “almost catatonic,” and caught a terrible cold.
Biden’s performance during the debate with Trump on June 27, 2024, at CNN’s Atlanta studio, was a historic disaster. Later that evening, at a debate watch party, Jill took the mike. “Joe, you did such a great job! You answered every question, you knew all the facts,” she said. “And what did Trump do?” She led the crowd with a shout of, “Lieee!”
Jill swiftly became a key focal point for the blame. Surely she had known how diminished he was, and if she knew, why had she not persuaded him to step down? That question could have been leveled against any number of people in the Biden orbit: top campaign aides, Kamala Harris, cabinet members. But as First Lady, she was the most intimate, public face of the campaign persuading Americans that he was fit to serve another term.
Many senior Democrats blamed her, along with the rest of the family and his close aides, for hiding his condition. At an event in Michigan that week, according to Jake Tapper and Alex Thompson in their book Original Sin, one of the state’s senators approached the First Lady for some indication of Biden’s real condition. “We don’t know . . . but you know.” Jill did not answer.
From THE EAST WING: Power, Intrigue, and the Untold Story of America’s First Ladies by Azadeh Moaveni. Copyright (c) 2026 by the author and reprinted with permission of St. Martin’s Press, an imprint of St. Martin’s Publishing Group.

news.title: Trump's Approval Rating in Senate Battlegrounds 2 Weeks Before Midterms
news.text: President Donald Trump’s approval rating remains low in Senate battlegrounds as Democrats and Republicans are engaged in a tight battle for control the upper chamber of Congress just two weeks before the midterm elections. Republicans are facing headwinds as they defend their majority, where they currently hold 53 seats to the Democrats’ 47. Trump’s approval rating, as well as voters’ views about the economy, have fueled a challenging national environment for the GOP two years after Trump’s victory in 2024. Why Trump’s Approval Rating Matters for the Midterms Historically, when the president is unpopular, his party loses seats in the midterms, and Democrats have been favored to retake the House this year. But the Senate has long been seen as a heavier lift. The Maine and North Carolina Senate seats were seen as clear pickups, but no other Republican-held seats were up for grabs in states Trump won by a single-digit margin or lost in 2024. As Trump’s approval rating has fallen, the Senate map has expanded for Democrats. The Cook Political Report lists seven races—Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas—as toss-ups. Trump’s approval rating is underwater in all of those states, according to Civiqs, which has tracked it in every state since the start of second term in January 2025. Whether or not those numbers improve over the next two weeks could play a role in the outcome of those races. Presidential approval is “one of the largest factors [if not the largest factor] driving voter behavior in a midterm election,” Jacob Neiheisel, political science professor at the University at Buffalo, told Newsweek. Neiheisel said he believes Trump’s poor approval numbers has given Democrats the ability to compete in tougher states. “In ‘wave’ elections, the out-party can play on the in-party's side of the field and win rates even in what are, from all outward appearances, safe seats are lower in such years,” he said. Many of those races appear to be close, he said, noting that “a good night for Democrats could mean walking away with quite a few of the toss-up Senate seats.” Whether or not the polls are off, however, will not be known until Election Day, he said. “They have been in recent presidential contests but have been pretty good in midterm races," he said. "There is always a chance, however, that they are missing something.” What Is Donald Trump’s Approval Rating? Trump’s approval ratings have created a headache for Republicans in the final stretch of the campaign, as candidates are making their final pitches to voters. A recent poll from Reuters and Ipsos revealed where Trump’s approval stood nationally. It found that his net approval rating was at -35 points, 31 percent approving and 66 percent disapproving, among 1,679 adults October 16-19, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.4 percentage points. Trump has criticized such polls. On August 30, he posted on Truth Social: “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT.” While Democrats believe they may be able to flip the Senate, there is always the possibility of a polling error that could benefit Republicans. In recent cycles, polling has not always been accurate. Republicans have at times overperformed polling averages in key races. Polling errors are not necessarily repeated from cycle to cycle, but a similar error this cycle would not bode well for Democrats’ chances of flipping the Senate. Here is a look at where Trump’s approval rating stands in key races, according to Civiqs. Alaska Although Trump won Alaska by about 13 points in 2024, his approval rating was -12 points—52 percent to 40 percent—in the latest numbers from Civiqs. Alaska has become less solidly conservative over the past few decades. As Democrats gain ground in cities like Anchorage and Fairbanks, Republicans’ statewide margins have narrowed from 31 points in 2000 to about 13 points in 2024 in presidential elections. GOP Senator Dan Sullivan is facing a challenge from former Representative Mary Peltola, the Democrat who represented the state's at-large district from 2022 to 2025. The latest polls show a close race. Peltola led by 2 points, 50 percent to 48 percent, in a survey from InsiderAdvantage conducted October 9-10 with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. A survey from The New York Times and Siena University showed Peltola up 7 points, 50 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 504 likely voters September 24-October 1, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5.1 percentage points. Trump recently campaigned in Alaska, and Sullivan has been supportive of the president. In an October 13 post to Truth Social, Trump described Sullivan as “one of the best and most respected” senators. Sullivan praised Trump in an October 13 post on X: “President Trump is the first president EVER to visit the Mat-Su Valley. If we turn out the Valley, then we turn out Alaska. And if we win Alaska, then we win America.” Iowa Trump’s approval rating in Iowa was -22 points, according to Civiqs, despite him winning the state by around 13 points in 2024. Thirty-four percent of Iowans approve of Trump, while 56 percent disapprove, according to the poll. Iowa was a battleground, backing President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012, before shifting rightward over the past decade, voting for Trump in all three of his presidential runs. Trump has become a major issue in the race between Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek. In Iowa, farmers stand to face impacts from Trump's tariffs and high diesel prices, as agriculture is a key part of the state’s economy. Turek was up 47 percent to 46 percent in a recent YouGov poll of 2,245 likely voters conducted October 6-12. However, an Emerson College poll showed Hinson with a 2-point lead, 47 percent to 45 percent, among 650 likely voters October 5-6. The YouGov poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, while Emerson's was 3.8. Hinson has walked a fine line on Trump and has put some distance between herself and the president on the issue of the Iran war. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices,” she wrote on September 21 on X. Trump has endorsed Hinson and is expected to visit Iowa. Kansas The Kansas race has become closer than initially expected. GOP Senator Roger Marshall has faced a series of close polls against Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton, and Trump has campaigned in Kansas to give Marshall a boost. Kansans were more split on Trump, with 46 percent disapproving and 45 percent approving, according to Civiqs. Trump won Kansas by about 16 points against former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. Marshall led Hamilton 48 percent to 47 percent in the latest InsiderAdvantage poll of 1,200 likely voters October 13-14. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Meanwhile, Hamilton held a 3-point lead in a YouGov poll of 2,253 likely voters September 24-October 4, with 48 percent support to the Republican’s 45 percent. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points. Marshall has touted his support from Trump, with his campaign previously telling Newsweek that he is a “president who is second to none at getting out the vote.” Maine In Maine, Senator Susan Collins is the only Republican running for reelection in a state that Trump lost in 2024, and she is facing difficult headwinds. Still, she has been able to make a close race due to her personal popularity and moderate image. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. Harris won Maine by 7 points in 2024. Two years later, Trump is 33 points underwater there, according to Civiqs. Only 30 percent of Mainers approve of Trump, while 63 percent disapprove. Collins has never been a particularly close Trump ally and has touted her record on breaking with Trump, such as voting down the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and some Cabinet nominees like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. However, Democrats have argued that she votes against him when her vote does not tip the scales. During a recent debate, Collins said she is “not exactly his favorite senator” when asked about whether Trump plans to visit Maine before the November 3 election. Collins’ reelection largely rests on her ability to win over ticket-splitters who backed Harris in 2024. A Suffolk University poll gave Jackson a 2-point lead, 49 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 500 Maine voters October 8-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Jackson was up 4 points among 800 likely voters in a poll from The Washington Post and George Mason University, conducted September 30-October 5. Fifty percent said they planned to vote for Jackson, while 46 percent intended to back Collins. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Michigan Michigan is the only Democratic-held Senate seat in the toss-up column. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican former Representative Mike Rogers are running to succeed retiring Democrat Gary Peters in a swing state Trump narrowly won in 2024. Trump is now less popular in Michigan, with 33 percent of voters approving of him and 61 percent disapproving, according to Civiqs. Democrats have hoped that the national environment would benefit them in swing states like Michigan, but polls have suggested the race is close. Republicans hope to cast El-Sayed, a progressive endorsed by independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, as too far left for a more moderate state. Rogers is another Republican who has been more willing to break with Trump. He has spoken out against Trump’s trade war with Canada and has called for an end to the Iran war. El-Sayed led by 4 points in a survey from Mitchell Research & Communications, 45.6 percent to 41.4 percent. It polled 682 likely voters October 1 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. A Fox News poll showed an even closer race, giving El-Sayed just a 1-point lead, 50 percent to 49 percent. It was conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research from September 24-28 among 1,028 likely voters. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Ohio Ohio, like Iowa, is a former midwestern battleground that has become more conservative in recent years but appears to be more competitive in this year’s elections. Trump won Ohio by about 11 points in 2024 but is now 21 points underwater, with 36 percent approving and 57 percent disapproving of him, per Civiqs. Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance, is facing a challenge from Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, who represented the state for nearly two decades before losing reelection in 2024. Brown held a 4-point lead in a Marist University poll, 48 percent to 44 percent, among 1,176 likely voters October 15-18, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. An ActiVote poll, which surveyed 400 likely voters September 26-October 18, showed the two candidates tied at 50 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. Husted has campaigned with Trump, though he has broken with the president in some instances, including voting against the anti-weaponization fund and calling for a quick end to the Iran war. Texas Texas’ reputation as a conservative stronghold is at risk as GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton faces a competitive challenge from Democratic state Representative James Talarico. Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024, but his approval has fallen to -21 points, with 36 percent approving and 57 percent disapproving, according to Civiqs. Paxton is a close Trump ally, and the president boosted his primary challenge against longtime Republican Senator John Cornyn by giving him an endorsement. Trump has rallied behind Paxton, and the MAGA Inc. PAC, which is aligned with the president, has invested heavily in the race as polls show Talarico with a slight edge. A YouGov poll showed Talarico up 2 points, 51 percent to 49 percent, among 1,458 likely voters October 8-16. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. A poll from the University of Houston also gave Talarico a 2-point lead, 48 percent to 46 percent, among 2,000 likely voters October 10-14, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.19 percentage points. Democrats’ Chances of Flipping the Senate, Two Weeks Before Election Day Democrats have emerged as favorites in prediction markets. On Kalshi, Democrats had a 63 percent chance of winning a majority on Tuesday, while they had a 65 percent chance on Polymarket. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. What Happens Next Trump’s approval rating will remain closely watched as an important gauge of the electorate’s mood in the final stretch of campaign season. His approval could be shaped by issues like the economy and cost of living over the coming weeks, as candidates continue to make their final pitches to voters ahead of the midterms. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Trump is unpopular in seven states with toss-up Senate races ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to polling data.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Sunny Hostin re-visits 'problematic' Kamala Harris answer on 'The View' as hosts question her 2028 potential
news.text: "The View" co-host Sunny Hostin revisited her widely-discussed 2024 question to former Vice President Kamala Harris during an event on Monday, calling the former Democratic presidential nominee's answer and refusal to distance herself from former President Joe Biden at the time "problematic." Brian Teta, the talk show's executive producer and host of its "Behind the Table" podcast, selected the moment as Hostin's most memorable on the show. He said it was a "seminal moment" in the 2024 election cycle. Hostin described the question as a "gift" and said she thought Harris would have to distance herself from Biden because of his approval ratings at the time. She also said "The View" was the perfect venue to ask the question, calling the liberal show's audience "her people." "I actually thought the answer was going to be, you know, ‘We had a lot of wins in this administration. I was there for those wins, but I, as a woman of color, as a child of immigrants, as I have a different lived experience, and I intend to bring that lived experience with me into the White House. I will do this. I will do that. I will do this. I will do that. I will do that.’ That was what I was expecting. I was not expecting, 'Not a single thing comes to mind.' And I knew honestly when she said it that it was really problematic," Hostin said. KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS The co-hosts noted that the moment was discussed in books published after the 2024 election, including Harris' memoir, "107 Days," and was also featured in a political ad for President Donald Trump. In "107 Days," Harris wrote that she had no idea she had just "pulled the pin on a hand grenade," with her answer to Hostin's question. She wrote that her staff was beside themselves. "Stationed at various places around the set, my staff were beside themselves. Political operatives have an eye to see a moment, and I could kick myself for giving the other side that moment. During the commercial break, while I was having a bit of fun with some young students I’d noticed in the audience who were obviously playing hooky, offering to write notes to their teachers after the show, Opal [Vadhan] passed me a note from our team, telling me to return to that question and mention that a big difference would be that I would put a Republican in my cabinet," she wrote in her book. 'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS CAST DOUBT ON KAMALA HARRIS VIABILITY AS 2028 CANDIDATE Teta and the co-hosts said they all knew her response was going to be a problem. Co-host Ana Navarro said Harris' staff "ran" because staff members knew immediately that Harris needed to return to the question and address her answer. KAMALA HARRIS FACES DEMOCRATIC DOUBTS OVER 2028 AS ALLIES PUSH BACK ON CLAIMS SHE’S SQUANDERED HER CHANCE During the show on Friday, both Navarro and Haines said they wouldn't tell Harris not to run, but questioned if she would be the best option for the Democratic Party. "If the Democrats want to win, I don't think she's the right candidate because I think the Democrats have been screaming for new energy. They've been saying we need something new to combat this. This would be her third time on this ballot. From the first time when she didn't ... she was out really early when she ran, and then the time with Biden, this would be the third time. People are clamoring for fresh energy, and there's a lot of candidates," Haines said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Co-host Joy Behar has said on several occasions that she doesn't think the U.S. would elect a woman as president, citing Harris and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's losses to Trump. She has said the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee should be a man if the party wants to win. Hostin questioned whether president would be the right position for Harris during an April episode of "The View" and said she wished Harris had pursued a run for California governor. "This goes right to the heart of what the Media Research Center has been arguing to the FCC about for months now. The View knowingly operates as a propaganda arm for the Democratic Party and for Democratic candidates," NewsBusters associate editor Nicholas Fondacaro told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Sunny openly admitted that her intention with the question was to help Kamala with what she felt was a layup question that would lead to a slam-dunk answer. This incident was an abuse of ABC's privileged access to the public broadcast spectrum."
news.summary: Sunny Hostin called Kamala Harris' answer on "The View" a "problematic" moment, revealing exactly what she expected the vice president to say.
news.author: Hanna Panreck

news.title: Warnock says Democrats are doing ‘barely enough’ in the South. He wants more.
news.text:
“Anger” isn’t a strong enough term for what Sen. Raphael Warnock said he’s seeing as he campaigns across four states in five days, mostly for Democratic Senate candidates in the South.

On Saturday, the tour brought Warnock to South Carolina to stump for Annie Andrews, the state’s Democratic Senate nominee. Flanked by Andrews and Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., he gave his signature sermon-style remarks to a crowd that included many of the state’s faith and Democratic leaders.

“The nation is just beginning to pay attention and wake up to what is happening in the South,” Warnock said. “In Mississippi … here in South Carolina … in North Carolina, there is a kind of righteous fury on the ground. The people of our country are saying enough is enough.”

With a conviction that reminded listeners that Warnock doubles as the senior pastor of Atlanta’s historic Ebenezer Baptist Church, the senator offered a solution.

“It’s time to turn the page. And it’s clear to me that the road to getting that done runs right through the South,” Warnock said. “As goes the South, so goes the nation.”

Warnock’s belief in the South’s untapped political potential comes from his own record. He won five elections in less than three years, repeatedly overcoming doubts that a Bible Belt Senate seat could flip to Democrats and stay that way. With the right political environment and enough investment, he argued, Southern Democrats can win races that look like long shots. He is pressing his party, including its Senate leadership, to act on that.

Over the past week, Warnock voted early in Georgia and joined Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor and Democratic nominee for governor, on the trail in Atlanta. He rallied Black men in Columbia and Charleston for Andrews, and he attended canvass launches in North Carolina for former Gov. Roy Cooper, the state’s Democratic Senate nominee.

But Mississippi’s Senate race seems to be most on Warnock’s mind. Without being asked, he brought up his support for Scott Colom, a district attorney trying to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Mississippi since 1982.

“I think when people hear ‘Mississippi,’ they make certain assumptions about what's possible, but they made those assumptions about Georgia,” Warnock said. “I think very often we lose by the margin of our disengagement.”

Warnock has hosted four fundraisers for Colom and helped raise more than $500,000 for him, his campaign told MS NOW. The campaign said that is more than any other senator has raised for a candidate. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., attended at least one of the fundraisers.

That hasn’t spared Schumer from Warnock’s prodding. Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Schumer, has praised Colom but has yet to make a significant investment in the race.

“We could do a lot better,” Warnock said. “I'm glad that the nation is finally waking up a little bit, paying attention to what's happening in the South. But I think that, to the degree that Democrats do just enough in the South, or barely enough, that we miss a real opportunity to do something transformational for the whole country.”

“I’m having that conversation with my colleagues all the time,” he added.

Warnock’s ambitions run up against political reality, though. Democrats are still weighed down by an unpopular national brand, and they raise significantly less money than Republicans. Asked whether it’s fair to expect the party to spend on races a Democrat hasn’t won in decades, Warnock began with a concession.

“There's no question that they have more money than we do. They always do. And if these policies persist, they always will,” he began. “Democrats' ceiling in the Senate is 52 seats. That's unsustainable. Over time, we have to expand the map. We can walk and chew gum at the same time. We can strengthen and shore up our candidates in places where people feel like we're more likely to win, and at the same time provide the kinds of resources that are needed to expand the map.”

Warnock argued that the “righteous fury” he keeps encountering can power those wins. He explained what he means by the phrase before heading from a Charleston fundraiser to Mother Emanuel AME Church, where a white supremacist killed nine Black worshipers in 2015.

“I think that this election is so much bigger than your typical election season, and the issues that confront our country are so much bigger than the puny language of partisan politics. That’s a kind of vocabulary that does not capture the moral moment,” Warnock said.

He pointed to outrage over a range of issues, from declining healthcare coverage rates to rising grocery costs to corruption “at the highest levels of government.”

“It’s the difference between right and wrong,” he said, “and I think people feel it on both sides of the aisle, which is why a state like South Carolina is at the center of this debate, and we can do something that seemed unimaginable not long ago in the Senate.”

Fifty-seven percent of eligible Black voters live in the South. The states where Warnock has spent the most time this week have among the highest shares of Black voters in the country. Warnock is also the senior pastor of Atlanta’s historic Ebenezer Baptist Church, where the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. preached, and he is seen as uniquely equipped to turn those voters out. That effort was on display Saturday, when he rallied supporters in predominantly Black North Charleston and Florence, South Carolina.

But Warnock said Democrats can’t rely only on turning out more of their most loyal voters. The party, he argued, must build a “multi-racial coalition” that crosses party lines. He said it should draw on outrage over what he called “cruel” Trump administration policies that target the most vulnerable.

That includes voters like Barbara Bates, 80, a lifelong Republican until recently, who came to hear Warnock and Andrews on Saturday. Bates voted for Donald Trump in 2016 but was turned off by “the way he’s so nasty to people.” She left the presidential line blank in 2020 and voted for Kamala Harris in 2024. Soon after, she was formally expelled from her local Republican party.

Bates isn’t ready to call herself a Democrat, but she shares Warnock’s diagnosis.

“Like he said, Washington's sick, and we need somebody to help fix it, and we just need more people that are willing to stand up to Trump,” Bates said.

Bates said Warnock’s faith could make him an especially valuable messenger in Bible Belt states like South Carolina, where nearly 80% of residents identify as Christian.

“The Republicans — to a certain extent the Christian nationalists have taken over,” she said. “They're running people away from the church, not to the church. People like Senator Warnock will be able to maybe let them think about where they really want to be and what Christianity really is.”

Warnock is betting that more voters like Bates can be persuaded to back Southern Democrats like Andrews. He’s also counting on polls showing public disapproval of the administration’s handling of issues including the war with Iran and immigration enforcement.

“What is different about this moment is that we have an administration that is wearing their bigotry on their sleeve,” Warnock said. “The cruelty that we're seeing unleashed, not only against Black people, but against people of color, against people who are perceived to be other — the cruelty is baked into the cake. It’s their electoral strategy.”

Warnock’s midterm travel this month has also taken him to New Hampshire and Nevada. Those two states and South Carolina have traditionally held some of the earliest contests on the Democratic presidential primary calendar. Asked about that, Warnock demurred.

“If you look at New Hampshire, South Carolina; those are places where we also have Senate candidates, or we need to win,” he said.

Pressed on whether he is at least considering a presidential run, Warnock wouldn’t do what his fellow Georgia Democrat, Sen. Jon Ossoff, has done: throw cold water on the idea.

“I am someone who's always had a deep sense of calling. I'm a pastor who didn't imagine that I'd be in the Senate, and my prayer has remained the same,” Warnock said. “How can I offer my resources, gifts, opportunities to serve in the best way at each moment?”

Whatever Warnock decides, he is up for re-election in 2028, and his next move will likely involve harnessing that “righteous fury.”

“I would like to see us channel that righteous fury, that sense of we’re better than this into a larger and nobler conversation,” he said. “We really are better than this, and I think we need leaders who can remind us of that.”
